Renewable Energy Foreign Direct Investment and Global Power Sector Green Transition: Micro-Level Evidence for Sustainable Development Abstract

Achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 (clean energy access) and SDG 13 (climate action)

requires understanding how international capital shapes national power sector transitions. Yet the role of

renewable energy foreign direct investment (FDI) in driving this transformation remains empirically

underdeveloped. Using a unique, manually constructed firm-project-level dataset of renewable energy

FDI spanning 185 countries over 2003–2023, this study provides novel micro econometric evidence on

how cross-border renewable energy investment affects the global power sector. We find that renewable

energy FDI significantly increases both the level and share of renewable electricity generation through

capital investment and job-creation channels, thereby accelerating the green transition of the power sector.

Heterogeneity analysis shows that these effects are strongest for wind and solar power, and more

pronounced in high-income economies than in low-income ones. Among project types, expansion and

co-location projects generate stronger employment and output effects than new investments, owing to

lower marginal costs and faster deployment on existing infrastructure. These findings extend the

Pollution Halo Hypothesis to the electricity sector and carry direct implications for global energy

governance: high-income countries should sustain green FDI incentives, while developing economies

must strengthen institutional and infrastructural conditions to fully capture the sustainable development

benefits of international renewable energy investment.

Keywords: Renewable energy; Foreign direct investment; Electricity sector; Green transition;

## 1. Introduction

Reducing costs, improving environmental quality, and creating new jobs have increased global

interest in energy transition—from traditional fossil fuels to renewable energy sources. In recent years,

supported by policy incentives, global renewable energy capacity has continued to expand, particularly

in wind and solar power. In 2023, global investment in renewable energy reached a record high of USD

622.5 billion, an 8.1% increase over 2022. Global renewable energy capacity additions are projected to

increase by 36% to 473 gigawatts, while 130 countries have committed to tripling their renewable energy

capacity by 2030 (REN21, 2024). Although cyclical fluctuations in global greenfield investment persist,

renewable energy – related greenfield investment is expected to sustain steady growth, driven by

technological innovation, policy support, and rising energy demand. Its share of total global greenfield

investment is also projected to increase (see Fig. 1). However, the role of international investment in

renewable energy has not been sufficiently examined in the existing literature. There is still a lack of

rigorous empirical evidence on whether renewable energy FDI can effectively promote the green

transition of the global electricity system. In this study, we precisely examine whether and how renewable

energy FDI affects global power sector green transition. In so doing, we use a unique firm project-level

global dataset of renewable energy FDI over a long period of time that combines project-level data and

national electricity generation data.

According to the World Investment Report 2024 (UNCTAD, 2024), the value of cross-border

greenfield project announcements in industries related to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)

increased by 14% in 2023, while the number of projects rose by an even larger margin of 19%. However,

this growth was mainly driven by a few key sectors—transport services accounted for roughly half of

the total increase in both project number and value, while renewable energy contributed about one-quarter.

Notably, although cross-border mergers and acquisitions have been declining, greenfield investment has

continued to expand, particularly in the renewable energy sector. Figure 2 further illustrates the changes

in the number of greenfield investment projects and the share of developing economies between 2011

and 2023. Overall, different economies have similar trends. From 2011 to 2019, global greenfield

investment remained relatively stable, but it rebounded significantly after 2020. The share of developing

economies in global greenfield projects increased from 33% in 2020 to 43% in 2023. This recovery is

closely linked to the rapid growth of FDI in the renewable energy sector in recent years, particularly in

clean energy projects such as solar, wind, and hydropower. Developing countries have attracted a

growing share of global renewable energy FDI, underscoring their rising importance in driving the global

energy transition.

This study defines "renewable energy FDI" as all investments made by multinational enterprises to

advance generation technologies, upgrade power infrastructure, and drive the structural transition of the

host country's electricity sector. The potential contribution of this study is the innovation of its research

object. Existing research mostly generalizes overall FDI to investigate its impact on energy consumption

(Shinwari et al., 2024), energy demand (Adom et al., 2019), and energy security (Fang et al., 2025), but

lacks specialized definition and detailed analysis of "renewable energy FDI". We first construct a unique

firm project-level global dataset of renewable energy FDI over a long period of time that combines

project-level data and national electricity generation data. The specific procedures are as follows. First,

we extract all energy-related projects from the fDi Markets database based on its “Sector” and “Cluster”

classifications. Second, using a “green investment for electricity generation only” identification strategy,

we manually code and classify each project by reviewing its source information to accurately identify

renewable energy FDI and analyze its specific effects. Third, the renewable energy FDI dataset is then

matched with national electricity generation data from the EIA by country and year, and organized into

a balanced panel dataset. Furthermore, considering the potential endogeneity that countries with higher

levels of green transition may be more likely to attract renewable energy FDI, we employ the system

generalized method of moments (System GMM) estimator and instrumental variable (IV) regression to

mitigate endogeneity concerns. Finally, we examine the heterogeneity effects of renewable energy FDI

by distinguishing among different types of renewable energy sources, countries at different income levels,

and various project types, focusing on their differential impacts on electricity generation, energy mix,

and job creation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature and

theoretical framework on the topic. Section 3 discusses methodology and data. Section 4 presents and

discusses empirical results. Section 5 concludes the paper.

## 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework

2.1. Literature Review

Given its central role in both energy consumption and carbon emissions, the electricity sector is

widely recognized as a critical lever for achieving carbon peaking and carbon neutrality targets. Existing

literature, both domestic and international, has largely concentrated on three core dimensions: FDI,

energy structure transition, and the low-carbon development of the electricity sector.

2.1.1. The FDI-energy Nexus

The primary linkage between FDI and energy lies in energy consumption. Yahya and Rafiq (2020)

finding that both greenfield and brownfield investments generally promote renewable energy

consumption. Doytch and Narayan (2016) found that FDI has a significant inhibitory effect on non-

renewable energy consumption, while it exerts a promoting effect on renewable energy consumption.

For instance, Salim et al. (2017) employed an ARDL (Autoregressive Distributed Lag) model to examine

the impact of FDI on energy consumption in China. Amoako and Insaidoo (2021) examined the

relationship between FDI and energy consumption in Ghana. More recently, Shinwari et al. (2024)

focused on economies along the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), finding that while FDI affects energy

consumption through green technology channels, it overall contributes to increased energy demand.

FDI can also affect energy consumption and efficiency to varying degrees across regions and sectors.

Using the Blundell-Bond dynamic panel estimation technique, Doytch and Narayan (2016) examined

data from 74 countries over the period 1985–2012. They found that sectoral FDI influx (manufacturing,

services, mining, and financial services) reduces non-renewable energy and augments renewable energy

consumption sources. However, the extent and significance of these impacts differ depending on the

sectoral composition of FDI. Adom et al. (2019) reported a non-linear relationship between FDI and

energy demand in Africa, suggesting the energy-saving benefits of FDI can only be realized when a

country possesses sufficient technological absorptive capacity. In China, Wei et al. (2020) explored how

FDI improves energy efficiency through mechanisms such as technology transfer and management

upgrading under diversified openness channels. In the long run, Salim et al. (2017) noted a significant

negative relationship between FDI and energy consumption, indicating that FDI may help curb energy

demand growth or enhance energy efficiency.

2.1.2. FDI and Green Development

The pollution haven hypothesis (Sapkota and Bastola, 2017) and the halo effect hypothesis (Hille

et al., 2019) provide important theories to explain the environmental effects of FDI. Empirical evidence

supports both hypotheses: Yahya and Rafiq (2020) demonstrated that both greenfield FDI and brownfield

FDI enhance renewable energy consumption. In countries with weak governance and high-risk

environments, brownfield investment can directly promote energy structure transformation, while

greenfield investment requires effective government performance to be effective. Tian et al. (2023)

finding that joint growth of inward and outward FDI significantly reduces industrial pollution—an effect

amplified by higher positioning in the global value chain. These contrasting perspectives highlight the

complex dynamics within the FDI–green–energy nexus.

The global energy structure is undergoing a major transition from fossil fuel dominance to

renewable energy. Within this process, green technology innovation (GTI) serves as a core driver for

reconciling economic growth with environmental objectives (Hossain et al., 2024). Shinwari et al. (2024)

emphasize the significance of FDI policies and green technologies in promoting energy demand in the

BRI economies. He et al. (2025) developed an evolutionary game model of heterogeneous firms under

IP protection to unravel the co-evolution of green innovation and energy transition. GTI can be assessed

along three dimensions: quantity, quality, and sustainability. This multidimensional perspective captures

the breadth, effectiveness, and long-term commitment of GTI, providing a more systematic basis for


<!-- Page 7 -->


understanding its role in advancing sustainable development (Wang et al., 2025).

2.1.3. FDI and Electricity Transition

FDI can promote the expansion and upgrading of electricity infrastructure in the host country,

thereby accelerating electricity transition and increasing electricity supply. D'Amelio et al. (2016)

revealed that multinational enterprises have significantly promoted electricity accessibility in Sub-

Saharan Africa, serving as an important external force for energy popularization and infrastructure

improvement. Using panel data from 36 Sub-Saharan African countries and applying the IV GMM

method, Aluko et al. (2023) found that FDI itself has a significant positive effect on improving electricity

coverage, and good governance can significantly enhance this positive impact of FDI.

Although existing literature has established a relatively rich theoretical and empirical foundation in

the fields of energy consumption, energy demand, and FDI, several important gaps remain unaddressed.

First, the classification of green FDI remains ambiguous. Many studies treat FDI as a homogeneous

variable, lacking a clear definition and in-depth analysis of “renewable energy FDI” which limits the

accurate identification of specific investment behaviors. Second, in the field of energy economics, current

research generally overlooks the close connection between renewable energy FDI and the green

transformation of the electricity sector, a key low-carbon industry. To contribute to this debate, this study

focuses specifically on renewable energy FDI rather than total FDI. Using panel data from 185 sovereign

countries over the period 2003–2023, the study systematically examines the role of renewable energy

FDI in promoting the global green transition of the electricity sector. Furthermore, we explore the

heterogeneous effects of renewable energy FDI from three dimensions: different energy type, income

level and the project type (including new, expansion, and co-location). To mitigate endogeneity concerns,

this study employed the system GMM estimator and the instrumental variables approach.

2.2. Theoretical Framework

This study develops a conceptual framework to clarify how renewable energy FDI affects the green

transition of the global power sector. As shown in Fig. 3, the framework links renewable energy FDI to

power sector transformation through two dimensions: direct effects and heterogeneous effects. These

pathways jointly form the basis for the research hypotheses proposed in this study.

2.2.1. Direct Effects of Renewable Energy Investment in the Power Sector

A successful renewable energy transition should prioritize local manufacturing, skills development,

energy funding and energy policy (Sen et al., 2025). Within the framework of endogenous growth theory,

multinational enterprises (MNEs) transfer advanced technologies and additional capital to host countries

through FDI, thereby stimulating economic growth. Therefore, FDI enhances production efficiency by

transferring valuable capital and technology, while the efficient mobility of production factors further

improves total factor productivity (TFP) in developing countries. In the context of green development,

the localized green R&D activities of MNEs in host countries facilitate the introduction of new clean

electricity generation technologies and the improvement of existing ones. Such activities accelerate the

construction and deployment of renewable energy projects—such as solar, wind, hydro, and biomass

power—thereby promoting the transition of the electricity sector from fossil-based to low-carbon energy

sources. Under such circumstances, FDI is regarded as an important driver of electricity access (Dogan

et al., 2024). Both developed and developing countries benefit from this process. Developed countries

gain through profit repatriation and continuous innovation in green electricity technologies, while the

effects are even more pronounced in developing countries. By leveraging foreign investment to build

green infrastructure and expand electricity access, these countries promote socioeconomic development

(Kanagawa & Nakata, 2008) and enhance labor productivity (Alam et al., 2018). Moreover, the green

transition process typically requires coordinated participation of multiple stakeholders. Evidence from

Infrastructure development plays a critical role in ensuring adequate electricity supply. Given the

strategic importance of electricity to business activities, MNEs often engage in the development of

electricity infrastructure to meet increasing demand (D'Amelio et al., 2016). Chen and Lin (2021) find

that the expansion of infrastructure will not only improve the energy services through direct effects but

also through the indirect effects of promoting economic growth. In fact, a substantial body of literature

has explored the relationship between FDI and factors such as economic growth, poverty reduction,

financial development, environmental regulation, and energy consumption. In recent years, many

scholars have become increasingly interested in the potential impacts of renewable energy FDI on host

countries. However, this relationship remains insufficiently explored, primarily due to the absence of a

comprehensive theoretical framework linking renewable energy FDI to the global power sector green

transition. To address this gap, the present study constructs a dataset of renewable energy FDI projects

to investigate their specific effects on the electricity sector and examines how three types of investment

behaviors — new, expansion, and co-location — contribute to the process of electricity sector

transformation.

Currently, the environmental impact of FDI is primarily explained by two competing hypotheses:

the Pollution Halo Hypothesis and the Pollution Haven Hypothesis (Eskeland and Harrison, 2003; Duan

and Jiang, 2021). The Pollution Halo Hypothesis suggests that FDI can improve the environmental

quality of host countries through technology spillovers, managerial expertise, and the transmission of

environmental standards. In contrast, the Pollution Haven Hypothesis posits that multinational

enterprises from developed economies tend to relocate pollution-intensive and energy-consuming

industries to developing countries with lax environmental regulations to avoid high compliance costs.

Together, these two hypotheses capture the essential relationship between foreign capital inflows and

environmental outcomes. Empirical evidence remains mixed. Keller and Levinson (2002) found that

reductions in production costs were associated with a decline in FDI in heavy manufacturing industries,

particularly in the chemical sector, while Wagner and Timmins (2009) confirmed the presence of the

pollution haven effect in the chemical industries of 163 countries. However, many of these studies are

based on aggregate FDI data and overlook the heterogeneity of investment motives and sector-specific

transmission mechanisms. This study examines the environmental effects of renewable energy FDI

across countries with different income levels. Since renewable energy FDI introduces advanced

technologies, capital inflows, and management practices, while also fostering the development of related

upstream and downstream industries—such as the manufacturing of turbines, hydropower equipment,

and solar panels—it is reasonable to assume that renewable energy FDI aligns more closely with the

Pollution Halo Hypothesis. Taking this into account, we propose Hypothesis 1.

Hypothesis 1: Renewable energy FDI promotes the global power sector green transition.

2.2.2. Heterogeneous Effects of Renewable Energy Investment in the Power Sector

Building on the analysis of direct effects, the heterogeneous impacts of renewable energy FDI on

the electricity sector can be summarized in three main dimensions.

(1) Different types of renewable energy exhibit substantial differences in resource endowments,

technological maturity, investment intensity, and grid integration constraints, leading to heterogeneous

marginal effects of renewable energy investment across generation technologies. Solar and wind projects

are characterized by relatively high technological maturity, strong modularity, and shorter construction

cycles. Once foreign capital enters, these projects can rapidly expand installed capacity and improve

generation efficiency through capital inflows, the introduction of advanced equipment, and the spillover

of managerial expertise (UNCTAD, 2024). Moreover, MNEs possess clear ownership advantages in

photovoltaic module production, wind turbine manufacturing, and system integration, which helps lower

technological barriers and alleviate financing constraints in host countries, thereby accelerating the pace

and magnitude of renewable energy structure optimization. In contrast, biomass projects rely heavily on

feedstock supply systems, regional agricultural structures, and logistics networks, and their technological

pathways and business models tend to be more localized. Although foreign investment can facilitate

project implementation to some extent, its marginal output effects are relatively limited. As a result, the

promoting effect of renewable energy FDI on biomass power generation is likely to be weaker than that

on solar and wind power. Taking this into account, we propose Hypothesis 2.

Hypothesis 2: Renewable energy FDI exhibits significant heterogeneity in its effects on different types

of electricity generation and its shares, with stronger impacts on solar and wind power.

(2) To balance economic development and sustainability, Ruan et al. (2025) advise improving

renewable energy investments, applying strict carbon pricing policies, and supporting technical

innovation. High-income countries possess greater financial resources to support technological

innovation, and green technologies represent a key means of reducing energy consumption, promoting

power structure transformation, and achieving sustainable development. As such, green technological

progress constitutes one of the most important channels through which renewable energy FDI exerts its

effects. Advances in green technology increase the substitutability of production factors, thereby raising

the marginal rate of substitution of traditional energy and facilitating the replacement of conventional

energy with cleaner alternatives (Gerstlberger et al., 2014). However, for middle-income and low-income

countries that face constraints in mobilizing fiscal resources, limitations in grid infrastructure, policy

continuity, and institutional quality persist. In these contexts, foreign investment projects may remain

largely at the level of capital inflows, making it difficult for them to fully generate technological

spillovers and structural upgrading effects, which in turn weakens the actual transition impact of

renewable energy FDI. Taking this into account, we propose Hypothesis 3.

Hypothesis 3: Renewable energy FDI has a more pronounced promoting effect in high-income countries,

while its impact is relatively weaker in low-income and middle-income countries.

(3) After MNEs complete their initial renewable energy investments, subsequent investment

decisions—such as expansion or co-location project—are jointly influenced by prior investment

experience, host-country market potential, and policy environment stability. On the one hand, home

countries can alleviate domestic resource constraints on economic growth and technological progress

through outward investment, generating cumulative investment effects and further attracting high-skilled

labor to engage in innovation activities, thereby fostering dynamic technological upgrading. On the other

hand, host countries benefit from capital inflows and advanced managerial expertise, which strengthen

learning and competition effects among local firms, reduce the risk of market monopolization, and

improve overall industry efficiency. As capital continues to accumulate, the density of projects increases,

gradually giving rise to regional energy industry clusters. This process not only significantly expands

employment but also promotes the green upgrading of the power sector by optimizing the electricity

supply structure and reducing carbon emissions, ultimately contributing to sustainable economic

development in developing countries. Large-scale photovoltaic investments in Pakistan have been shown

to play a positive role in advancing the host country’s energy transition (Aqeeq et al., 2023). However,

these effects depend on project types. New projects typically involve multiple stages, including site


<!-- Page 11 -->


approval, infrastructure construction, and grid connection upgrades, which entail high upfront fixed costs

and long construction periods. As a result, their investment effects are difficult to fully translate into

electricity output and employment growth in the short term, although they exhibit strong long-term

potential once projects become operational. In contrast, expansion projects and co-location projects rely

on existing power facilities, mature technological pathways, and stable market networks, enabling

capacity expansion and factor allocation at lower marginal costs. Consequently, their investment effects

are more likely to be reflected in short-term increases in electricity generation, improvements in the

power mix, and job creation. Taking this into account, we propose Hypothesis 4.

Hypothesis 4: Among different project types, expansion projects and co-location projects exert

significantly stronger promoting effects on power sector green transition and job creation than new

projects.

## 3. Empirical Strategy and Data

3.1. Empirical Methodology

This study examines the impact of renewable energy FDI on the green transformation of the global

electricity industry, utilizing both static and dynamic models. The static fixed effects model cannot

adequately address the potential endogeneity concerns in this study. Countries with better green power

transition may attract more FDI, rather than FDI causing the transition. The dynamic GMM estimation

method is well-suited to mitigate endogeneity and other econometric challenges commonly encountered

in empirical economic research. To further ensure the robustness of the results, an instrumental variables

approach is subsequently employed for validation.

3.1.1. Static Model

The static panel model is constructed in Eq.(1) using the findings from prior research conducted by

Razzaq et al. (2023). Renewable energy projects such as wind farms and photovoltaic power plants

typically involve long construction and commissioning periods, resulting in a time lag between capital

investment and its realization in electricity generation and power structure adjustment. To account for

this lag effect, this study uses a one-period lag of renewable energy FDI as the core explanatory variable.

Consequently, it aligns investment timing with observed electricity outcomes and captures the delayed

impact of renewable energy FDI on the green transition of the power sector.

The dynamic panel model of the System generalized method of moments (GMM) is also utilized to

3.2. Variables

Core independent variables: renewable energy FDI, measured as the Total capital investment of all

selected renewable projects. The capital investment is typically used as an indicator of project scale in

FDI analysis. FDI projects are classified into three project types: new, expansion and co-location.

Dependent variable: (1) Share of renewable energy generation (Ren_share): renewable energy is a

feasible alternative to fossil fuels. Compared with fossil fuels, renewable energy has the advantages of

renewability and environmental friendliness, while fossil fuels are the main contributors to carbon

emissions (Li et al., 2025). This study defines Ren_share as the proportion of renewable energy

generation in total electricity generation, which can more intuitively reflect the energy structure and the

degree of green transition in the electricity industry; (2) Renewable energy generation (Ren): To further

analyze the relationship between the scale of renewable energy development and renewable energy FDI,

this study also uses the absolute value of Ren as a dependent variable. This indicator can more directly

reveal the impact of renewable energy FDI on the expansion of actual generation capacity and helps to

understand its policy and economic implications from the perspective of scale; (3) Fossil fuel electricity

generation and its share (Fos, Fos_share); (4) Wind power generation and its share (Win, Win_share); (5)

Solar power generation and its share (Sol & Sol_share); (6) Hydropower generation and its share (Hyd,

Hyd_share). These various types of electricity generation help identify the specific impacts of renewable

energy FDI on different energy sources.

Control variable: Guided by existing studies (Garrone et al., 2019), this study includes the following

control variables: (1) GDP (constant 2015 US$). GDP is used to capture the economic development,

measured as the log of real GDP; (2) Total population. The Population growth of a country also impacts

public investments in renewable energy, measured as the log of real population; (3) Trade (% of GDP).

In general, a higher degree of economic openness enables a country to better facilitate the technological

spillover effects of FDI. Trade is measured as total trade (exports plus imports) as percentage of GDP;

(4) Urban population. It is used to indicate the level of urbanization, which may affect energy demand

patterns and infrastructure development; (5) Inflation, consumer prices (annual %). Used to reflect

macroeconomic stability. Its fluctuations may influence investment behavior and the risk assessment of

renewable energy projects; (6) Inflation, GDP deflator (annual %). As a broad indicator of price level

changes and the macroeconomic environment, it complements the CPI by capturing the potential impact

of inflation on energy production and investment.

3.3. Data

This study uses project databases from the fDi Markets for the period 2003-2023, which is

maintained by the Financial Times (UK), officially published by fDi Intelligence. This database is the

most comprehensive source of project-level cross-border greenfield investments available, covering all

countries and sectors worldwide since 2003. This unbalanced panel data contains a wide range of

indicators, including the name of the firm engaging in FDI, the year of investment, the capital investment,

the name of the destination country and source country, the recipient industry sector, the project type, the

jobs created and the source URL. Numerous studies have employed this database to investigate


<!-- Page 13 -->


Greenfield FDI (Yahya and Rafiq, 2020). fDi Markets is the primary source of greenfield FDI data for

various international organizations, consultancies, major corporations and over 100 governments

(Desbordes and Wei, 2017). Moreover, the unbalanced nature of fDi Markets implies that the industry

distribution of FDI projects may vary across countries, and the entry time of different countries into the

sample is not fixed. In our study, the most critical step is how to extract global renewable energy FDI

projects from the database. We follow a multi-step manual filtering and cleaning procedure, detailed as

follows.

First, we filter projects from the fDi Markets database using various classification criteria. We

exports all global project data from 2003 to 2023. Based on the “Cluster” classification, we select projects

categorized under “Energy” and “Environmental Technology”, resulting in 18,946 entries. Alternatively,

filtering by the “Sector” classification yields 12,321 records. However, these preliminary results may

include both renewable and non-renewable energy projects. To enhance the accuracy of the dataset, we

further manually verify each project by reviewing the “Source URL” field, which provides links to the

original source of information. By clicking and inspecting each source, we classify projects into three

categories: renewable energy FDI (coded as 1), non-renewable energy FDI (coded as 0), and uncertain

cases (coded as 2). A project is identified as renewable energy FDI if it involves the construction of new

renewable power plants, manufacturing of renewable energy equipment (wind turbines or photovoltaic

modules), or reinvestment at existing renewable energy sites. Projects with inaccessible links due to

outdated URLs are marked as uncertain. All remaining projects are considered non-renewable energy

FDI. Ultimately, 7,155 projects are confirmed as renewable energy FDI. Based on this refined dataset,

this study constructs a panel dataset of global renewable energy FDI from 2003 to 2023. We aggregate

the following key variables by country and year: (1) the Total capital investment of all selected renewable

energy projects (core independent variable); (2) the number of renewable FDI projects; (3) the number

of new jobs created; (4) the capital investment categorized by project type (new, expansion, and co-

location).

Second, we match the renewable energy FDI dataset with global electricity generation data by

country and year. The electricity generation data is sourced from the EIA, which provides comprehensive

coverage across countries and regions. This dataset includes not only total electricity generation but also

disaggregated generation by energy type (like fossil fuels and renewables), offering insight into each

country's energy structure and its evolution over time. We collect national data on total electricity

generation, fossil fuel generation and renewable energy generation, and calculate the share of each energy

source in total electricity generation. The share of renewable energy generation serves as our core

dependent variable.

Third, we clean the merged dataset as follows:(a) If renewable energy FDI data is missing, we treat

it as zero, indicating no renewable energy FDI occurred that year; (b) If electricity generation data is

missing, it is also set to zero, indicating no electricity generation activity that year; (c) We exclude

countries with no recorded electricity generation throughout the entire study period, as they lack an active

power sector and cannot be meaningfully evaluated for green transition; (d) We remove regional or

organizational-level observations, retaining only country-level data to ensure consistency and

comparability. After the above processing, the final dataset comprises 3,885 observations across 185

sovereign countries. Moreover, since Ren_share is lagged by one period and used as an instrumental

variable in the GMM model, the empirical analysis covers the period from 2004 to 2023. Descriptive

statistics of the variables are presented in Table 2.

## 4. Estimation Results

4.1. Baseline Estimates

*Table 3 reports the baseline results for Eq (1). Columns (1) and (3) use renewable energy generation*

(Ren) and its share as the dependent variables. Columns (2) and (4) further introduce all control variables

to test the robustness of the results. In all models, the coefficient of the core independent variable Cit is

positive and statistically significant at the 1% or 5% level. This indicates that foreign investment in the

renewable energy sector and the expansion of power generation capacity can promote the green transition

of the power structure. This finding is consistent with previous research by Kushawaha (2025), which

suggests a U-shaped relationship between greenfield FDI and renewable energy capacity, and a positive

effect of M&A FDI on renewable energy capacity. Specifically, an additional USD 1 billion in renewable

energy FDI is associated with an average increase of approximately 2.034 billion kWh in renewable

energy generation, and an increase of about 0.002 percentage points in its share in total generation. These

effects remain robust even after controlling for macroeconomic and structural factors.

After including control variables (Columns 2 and 4), the adjusted R² values increase, indicating

improved explanatory power of the models. The results show that lnGDP is significantly positively

associated with renewable energy generation (Ren), suggesting that higher levels of economic

development are linked to greater use of renewable energy generation. However, GDP exhibits a

significant negative effect on Ren_share, implying that in more developed economies, despite higher

absolute renewable energy generation, its share may remain limited due to the dominant role of

conventional energy sources. This outcome is consistent with that found in Sarkodie et al. (2020). Total

population and trade openness generally show significant negative coefficients, suggesting that countries

with larger populations and more open economies face greater pressure on energy supply or a stronger

reliance on fossil fuels in their energy transition. Urbanization is significantly positively associated with

Ren, reflecting how urban expansion may drive investment in energy infrastructure and renewable

technologies. However, urbanization has a significantly negative effect on Ren_share, indicating that

rapid urbanization may initially increase reliance on traditional energy sources. Lastly, the coefficients

of the consumer price index and GDP deflator are statistically insignificant in most specifications,

suggesting that these models do not provide evidence of a systematic association between short-term

price fluctuations and the renewable energy outcomes examined.

4.2. Panel Unit Root Test

The HT test was used to conduct the unit root test for short panel data. This test is designed to

analyze first-order autoregressive panel data models with serially uncorrelated errors, where N

approaches infinity (N→∞) while T remains constant (Harris and Tzavalis, 1999). Table 4 conducts the

HT test on all variables except the share of generation, primarily because ratio-type variables typically

range between 0 and 1, are generally considered stationary by nature. The results show that, except for

solar and wind generation, all other variables pass the HT test, indicating a good degree of stationarity.

While some variables (such as Job and Expc) do not initially meet the criteria, they become stationary

after first-differencing. Due to an insufficient number of non-zero observations, solar and wind

generation could not be subjected to the unit root test; however, this does not affect the subsequent

empirical analysis.

4.3. Endogeneity Tests: System GMM and IV Results

Following the approach of Berk et al. (2020), this study employs the System GMM for dynamic

panel data, combined with the instrumental variable approach, to mitigate potential endogeneity concerns.

*Table 5 presents three models: Models (1) and (2) are based on system GMM, with Model (2) including*

full control variables. Model (3) applies an instrumental variables (IV) approach using internet

penetration and the rule of law index as instruments. Across all specifications, Cit remains positively and

significantly associated with the Ren_share, confirming its role in promoting a greener electricity

structure. The lagged dependent variable L.Ren_share is also significantly positive, suggesting a strong

path dependency in green electricity transition—earlier progress tends to persist over time. From a

robustness perspective, the AR (1) test shows significant first-order autocorrelation, while the AR (2) test

is insignificant, indicating the absence of second-order autocorrelation. The Hansen test fails to reject the

null hypothesis, supporting the validity of the instruments in the GMM estimation. Internet penetration

measures the extent of digital and communications infrastructure development across countries, as

captured by the share of individuals using the internet. This study uses internet penetration and the rule

of law index as instrumental variables (Deng et al., 2024), based on two main reasons: (1) Well-developed

internet infrastructure and a sound legal environment help attract green FDI; (2) Internet and the rule of

law index are not directly related to the share of renewable energy generation. The instrumental variable

regression results further confirm the positive impact of renewable energy FDI on the transformation of

the electricity structure toward renewables. The Hansen test results indicate that the instruments are valid,

and the model passes both the Kleibergen-Paap LM test and the Stock-Yogo weak instrument critical

value test, suggesting that the instruments are strong and the model is well-identified. It supports the

overall robustness of the model.

4.4. Robustness tests

In this section, robustness of our findings is assessed through several approaches. Specifically, we

conduct robustness checks by employing lagged variables, adjusting the sample scope, and replacing the

dependent variable.

4.4.1. Lagged Variable Test

First, to account for the potential lagged effects of renewable energy FDI (Cit) on the electricity

structure, this study re-estimates the model by introducing one-year, two-year, and three-year lags of the

core explanatory variable (see Table 6). The estimation results indicate that the coefficient of renewable

energy FDI remains significantly positive across all lag specifications, with the significance level

essentially unchanged. This suggests that the positive effect of renewable energy FDI on expanding

renewable electricity generation and increasing its share in the electricity mix is not confined to the

contemporaneous period but persists over a longer horizon. Furthermore, in the two-year and three-year

lag specifications, the signs of the coefficients are consistent with those of the baseline estimates, and the

magnitude changes are minimal. These results provide further evidence supporting the robustness of the

baseline findings and demonstrate the sustained nature of the positive impact of renewable energy FDI.

4.4.3. Alternative Dependent Variable Test

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) classification, power generation sources can

be divided into two categories: renewable energy and fossil fuels. To examine the impact of renewable

renewable energy FDI helps host countries reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, particularly high-

may be accompanied by parallel investments in natural gas projects, such as joint peak-load regulation

and flexible generation. It highlights that the green transition is a gradual substitution process rather than

and increases the share of renewable energy, promoting the green transformation of the global electricity

4.5. Heterogeneity Analysis

In this section, we discuss the heterogeneity in the impact of renewable energy FDI on the green

transition of the global electricity sector from three perspectives: differences in energy types, differences

in national income levels, and differences in project types with respect to both renewable energy FDI

effects and employment effects.

4.5.1. Renewable Energy Type

*Table 9 estimates the effects of renewable energy FDI from two perspectives—different generation*

and its share—to further examine its impact on different types of renewable energy, namely solar (Sol,

Sol_share), wind (Win, Win_share), and biomass (Bio, Bio_share). The results show that renewable


<!-- Page 21 -->


energy FDI has a significantly positive effect on all three energy types, both in terms of absolute

generation and share in the power mix. This indicates that renewable energy FDI plays an active role in

promoting the diversification of renewable energy sources. Specifically, each additional USD 1 billion

in renewable energy FDI is associated with an average increase of approximately 697 million kWh in

solar power generation and 1.232 billion kWh in wind power generation, as well as an increase of about

0.001 percentage points in their respective shares of the electricity structure. This suggests that renewable

energy FDI has strongly supported the development of solar infrastructure—particularly in emerging

economies where investment in solar technologies has grown rapidly in recent years. In countries rich in

wind resources, foreign capital has also facilitated the construction of wind farms, the introduction of

equipment, and the diffusion of wind power technologies. Although the marginal effect of FDI on

biomass energy is comparatively smaller, it remains statistically significant. This confirms that renewable

energy FDI has also played a positive role in driving biomass energy projects. Ramanauske et al. (2023)

demonstrated, through case studies of European countries, the contribution of biomass energy utilization

to economic structural transformation and the optimization of energy systems. In sum, renewable energy

FDI contributes not only to the overall green transformation of the electricity sector but also to the

technological development and synergy of renewable energy, with particularly strong marginal effects

observed in the solar and wind sectors. This provides important guidance for policymakers when

formulating investment-oriented policies in specific energy sub-sectors.

4.5.3. Project Type

To further examine heterogeneity across project types, we divide renewable energy FDI into three

Using the amount of capital investment as the proxy, three types of investment variables are constructed,

namely Cin, Cie, and Cil. This study estimates their respective effects on renewable energy generation

value, but their output tends to experience greater delays. Expansion and co-location projects exhibit

stronger efficiency and more pronounced short-term impacts.

4.5.4. Employment Effects by Project Type

Foreign direct investment can significantly promote employment growth in the host country,

including direct, indirect, and induced employment (Zhao et al., 2024). Building upon this, the present

study further explores the employment effects of renewable energy FDI across different project types.

As shown in Table 12, the empirical results indicate that renewable energy FDI has an overall

significantly positive effect on job creation, with an additional USD 1 billion in renewable energy FDI

is associated with approximately 243 new jobs. However, considerable heterogeneity exists among

project types. Specifically, co-location projects exhibit the strongest marginal employment effects,

creating around 2127 jobs per USD 1 billion—substantially higher than new and expansion projects. This

may be attributed to the fact that co-location projects are typically implemented using existing

infrastructure, labor, and technological capacity, thereby achieving higher capital conversion efficiency

and greater employment absorption. This finding aligns with the results reported in Table 11. Co-location

projects not only promote renewable energy generation but also significantly enhance employment

outcomes. In contrast, new projects often require longer construction periods and are more reliant on

automation, resulting in lower employment intensity per unit of investment. Policymakers may consider

project-type heterogeneity when designing renewable energy investment policies, while balancing short-

## 5. Conclusions and implications

Electricity is a marker for development (Dinkelman, 2011). Since 2010, global renewable electricity

generation has shown a sustained upward trend, with its share rising markedly after 2015. This evolution

aligns closely with the accelerated implementation of global low-carbon transition policies, including the

signing of the Paris Agreement, the official launch of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals,

and the introduction of renewable energy development strategies and targets by many countries. These

policy frameworks not only provide clear institutional guidance but also significantly enhance national

incentives for renewable energy investment and deployment. Unlike previous studies that primarily focus

on overall FDI, the main innovation of this study lies in the explicit definition and precise identification

of renewable energy FDI among various types of FDI. We manually screen and identify renewable energy

FDI projects worldwide to construct a firm-level global dataset covering 185 sovereign countries from

2003 to 2023, which is then matched with electricity generation data from the U.S. Energy Information

Administration. This enables a systematic examination of the mechanisms through which renewable

energy FDI contributes to the green transition of the global power system.

Our findings remain consistent and significant across various model specifications and robustness

checks. Based on the static two-way fixed effects model, the estimates show a statistically significant

positive association between renewable energy FDI and both renewable electricity generation and its

share in the power mix. In addition, by employing the system GMM dynamic panel model and

instrumental variable approach, we alleviate potential endogeneity concerns arising from the possibility

that countries with faster green transition processes may themselves attract more foreign investment.

The heterogeneity analysis reveals that the diversification of electricity generation sources provides

additional momentum for the green transition, gradually facilitating the substitution of fossil fuels with

renewable energy. Among different energy types, renewable energy FDI exerts the most significant

marginal effects on wind and solar power, indicating its crucial role in promoting the diversification of

clean energy development, whereas its impact on biomass energy is relatively weaker. Furthermore, the

technological effect of renewable energy FDI is found to be more pronounced in high-income countries.


<!-- Page 25 -->


This may be attributed to several factors, including the fact that high-income economies typically possess

more advanced power infrastructure, well-established environmental governance systems, and greater

capacity to leverage cutting-edge technologies and financial resources through foreign direct investment.

At the project level, this study documents an interesting finding: different types of renewable energy FDI

projects exert varying impacts on both the green transition of the electricity sector and the creation of

new employment opportunities. The results indicate that expansion and co-location projects exhibit larger

short-run coefficients for renewable electricity outcomes and employment than new projects. This

suggests that expansion projects can capitalize on existing electricity infrastructure to achieve rapid

capacity scaling and optimize the green composition of the power mix, while co-location projects take

advantage of existing geographic locations, resources, and technological assets to exhibit higher capital

conversion efficiency. This finding is consistent with IRENA's (2023) emphasis on an “efficiency-

oriented reinvestment pathway”, particularly suitable for countries and regions with well-established

institutions and stable policy environments. In contrast, while greenfield projects hold important strategic

value in the medium to long term, they typically involve longer construction cycles, create fewer new

jobs, and yield lower short-term returns. Therefore, when formulating future policies on renewable

energy FDI, countries should consider the project life cycle, underlying infrastructure conditions, and

policy environment in a comprehensive manner, to better realize the scale effects of investment. By doing

so, they can not only safeguard long-term strategic objectives but also ensure better alignment between

project types and timeliness, thereby achieving dual optimization in resource allocation and green

transition (World Bank, 2023).

As shown by Xu and Sun (2025), heterogeneity across groups is critical for the effectiveness of

policy interventions. For developing countries, improving internet penetration, institutional quality, and

the rule of law may enhance their capacity to attract and utilize renewable energy FDI, thereby

accelerating the energy transition and creating jobs. For developed countries, renewable energy FDI can

further stimulate technology spillovers and innovation activities, supporting long-term green growth. At

the global level, the positive role of renewable energy FDI not only aligns with the United Nations

Sustainable Development Goals but also holds significant importance for fostering a more inclusive and

sustainable global energy transition.

This study has several important limitations that should be acknowledged. First, our analysis draws

exclusively on greenfield investment records from the fDi Markets database, and cross-border mergers

and acquisitions in renewable energy are not incorporated into our empirical setting. As a result, we

cannot capture the full scope of cross-border renewable energy FDI. Second, while we isolated renewable

energy FDI, we did not disaggregate it into specific sub-sectors (e.g., wind, solar, or biomass). This limits

our capacity to evaluate the heterogeneous effects of diverse green capital flows. Third, despite deploying

system-GMM and instrumental variable specifications to alleviate endogeneity risks, observational panel

data cannot fully rule out omitted-variable bias or reverse causality. Fourth, our analysis focuses on

aggregate country-level outcomes. We cannot capture within-country regional disparities. Accordingly,

future research can advance this work in multiple directions. Further work may integrate M&A

transaction data to compare greenfield and brownfield renewable energy investment impacts. Subsequent

studies may also adopt finer sub-sector classifications and sub-national regional data. More granular

identification strategies are needed to sharpen causal inference and disentangle the exact transmission

mechanisms linking cross-border renewable energy capital inflows to power-sector decarbonization.

# Exploratory task-specific evaluation of large language models in lung cancer clinical scenarios: A comparative study

**Authors:** Wenzheng Zhang; Xue Li; Run Yuan; Yinuo Zhang; Yufei Yang; Yun Xu; Ruikang Zhong; Siyi Chen; Dianna Liu; Lei Gao; Kaiwen Hu

**Affiliations:** 1Graduate School, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, Beijing, China | 2Department of Oncology, Xiyuan Hospital, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, Beijing, China | 3Department of Medical Biochemistry and Microbiology, Science for Life Laboratory, Biomedical Center, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden | 4Institute of Basic Research in Clinical Medicine, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, Beijing, China | 5Graduate School, Chongqing Medical School, Chongqing, China | 6Dongfang Hospital, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, Beijing, China

## Abstract

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok, have shown promise in clinical decision support, but differences in training and alignment may lead to variable performance. Current evaluations often rely on aggregate metrics or isolated tasks, which may not capture real-world clinical complexity.

We conducted a structured evaluation of three LLMs using nine simulated lung cancer cases across five clinical domains. LLMs’ outputs were anonymized, randomized, and independently scored by five senior lung cancer specialists under a double-blind design using a five-point Likert scale evaluating accuracy, comprehensiveness, relevance, and clinical applicability. Qualitative error analysis was also performed.

Inter-rater agreement was moderate (Fleiss’ κ = 0.463; ICC (2, k) = 0.675). All LLMs achieved high scores across evaluation dimensions without statistically significant differences (P > 0.05). Given the limited number of simulated cases, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Descriptive analyses suggested context-dependent performance patterns across clinical domains: Grok tended to show more consistent performance in diagnosis and treatment decision-making, DeepSeek showed comparatively lower descriptive performance in therapeutic decisions but higher applicability in prognosis and rehabilitation, and GPT exhibited relatively stable intermediate performance. No single LLM consistently outperformed others across all clinical scenarios.

LLMs demonstrate substantial potential in supporting lung cancer clinical workflows, but their performance appears to be context-dependent. The present findings are exploratory and suggest that task-specific evaluation may provide a more clinically informative framework than overall model ranking. Continued validation using larger and more diverse clinical datasets, together with appropriate governance and specialist oversight, remains essential for the safe integration of LLMs into clinical practice.

Keywords: lung cancer, large language model, evaluation, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok

## Introduction

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, responsible for an estimated 1.8 million deaths annually. 1 Accurate diagnosis, appropriate staging, timely treatment decisions, and effective patient communication are critical to delivering high-quality lung cancer management. 2 However, the implementation of these processes requires the integration and interpretation of increasingly complex multidimensional information, including imaging findings, pathological features, molecular alterations, treatment history, and individual patient factors.3–6 In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to support clinical workflows, particularly through large language models (LLMs), which exhibit advanced capabilities in natural language understanding and medical reasoning. 7

Mainstream LLMs such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok have demonstrated remarkable potential across various medical tasks,8–10 including clinical question answering, evidence summarization, patient education, and even simulated clinical consultations. 8 Foundational studies of medically adapted LLMs have further shown that these models can achieve expert-level performance on medical reasoning and clinical question-answering benchmarks, highlighting their potential to support evidence-informed clinical decision-making. 11 Unlike traditional clinical decision-making, which primarily relies on individual physicians whose access to updated knowledge, continuous training, and medical resources can be constrained by economic conditions and regional disparities, LLMs have the potential to synthesize large volumes of biomedical knowledge and assist clinicians in accessing evidence and guideline-informed recommendations.11–16

Beyond individual clinical decision-making, LLMs also have the potential to address broader healthcare system challenges. In many regions, particularly in low-resource settings, access to experienced oncologists and multidisciplinary teams remains limited, contributing to disparities in cancer outcomes. By providing guideline-informed recommendations and scalable decision support, LLMs may help extend oncology expertise beyond tertiary centers, improve consistency of care, and enhance patient education. Therefore, evaluating LLM performance in realistic clinical scenarios is not only relevant for individual patient management but also for understanding their potential role in improving equity and efficiency in cancer care delivery at the population level. 17

In lung cancer care, where treatment decisions often involve complex genomic profiles, multimodal therapies, and rapidly evolving evidence, LLMs may assist in generating differential diagnoses, recommending guideline-concordant treatment options, anticipating side effects, and providing clear explanations to patients.18,19 These strengths position LLMs not as replacements for human clinicians but as augmentative tools that can enhance decision-making accuracy, reduce disparities, and improve patient outcomes. 20

However, given that these models differ significantly in terms of training data sources, linguistic-cultural orientation, model architecture, and alignment strategies, it is crucial to examine whether and how these differences affect clinical outputs in real-world medical scenarios. 20 Previous studies have shown that different LLMs exhibit variable performance across medical reasoning, clinical question answering, and clinical decision-support tasks, highlighting the need for task-specific evaluation in specialized clinical settings.9,10,21–26

In the era of rapidly evolving artificial intelligence technologies, comparative analyses of different LLMs are essential to move beyond isolated model development toward evidence-based selection, clinical translation, and standardized evaluation in lung cancer management. Recent studies have indicated that LLMs such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek show highly promising potential in various medical applications, including clinical decision support for breast cancer, colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and neonatal care. However, each model also exhibits specific limitations in areas such as diagnostic accuracy, treatment precision, response time, and report generation quality.10,27–29 Therefore, understanding the performance gap between these LLMs is not only methodologically relevant but also clinically imperative.30,31 Comparative evaluations research can help guide appropriate model selection and provide evidence-based recommendations for deployment. 31 Furthermore, such research contributes to the development of standardized evaluation frameworks for AI tools in medicine and supports regulatory and ethical oversight. Additionally, it offers insights into the design of future domain-specific LLMs optimized for clinical safety, accuracy, and equity.

However, current research has largely focused on overall performance comparisons or isolated question-answering tasks, often emphasizing aggregate scores or model ranking.32–37 Such approaches may not adequately reflect the heterogeneity of real-world clinical practice, where different tasks, such as diagnosis, treatment decision-making, symptom management, and patient communication, place distinct demands on AI systems. A model that performs well in guideline interpretation may not demonstrate equivalent reliability in patient counseling or complex decision-making contexts. Therefore, structured, scenario-based evaluation is needed to better understand task-specific strengths and limitations.

Therefore, we conducted a structured comparative analysis of several widely used LLMs, including ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok using nine simulated lung cancer cases across five clinical domains. LLM outputs were assessed by a multidisciplinary panel using four dimensions: accuracy, comprehensiveness, relevance, and applicability. This study aims to provide clinically meaningful insights into LLM performance and support their appropriate integration into lung cancer care.

## Materials and methods

### Study design

This study employed a structured and mixed-methods design to assess the performance of GPT, Grok, and DeepSeek LLMs in the clinical lung cancer clinical scenarios. We assembled an expert panel of five lung cancer specialists, each with ≥10 years of experience: one thoracic surgeon, one medical oncologist, one radiation oncologist, one rehabilitation specialist, and one senior oncology nurse.

All LLM responses were generated between February 18 and March 25, 2026, with each simulated case submitted once to each model during this predefined evaluation period. All nine clinical cases were evaluated using the most recent publicly available versions of GPT-5.4, Grok 4.1, and DeepSeek-V3.2. Responses were regenerated using a standardized prompting strategy and re-evaluated by five experts under identical conditions. All responses were generated via cloud-based APIs (no on-premises deployment or integration with local patient data systems). All cases were originally presented in English.

### Design, classification, and evaluation of simulated clinical scenarios

Five key clinical domains were selected with reference to major international guidelines, including the NCCN, ESMO, and CSCO recommendations, as well as standard multidisciplinary team (MDT) workflows commonly adopted in tertiary medical centers worldwide: (1) diagnosis and assessment; (2) treatment decision-making; (3) symptom management; (4) psychosocial support; and (5) rehabilitation guidance and prognosis. To enhance clinical granularity, the five major domains were further subdivided into eight clinically distinct subdomains, with detailed mapping provided in Supplementary material 1.

The simulated cases were not derived from individual patient records but were developed by two experienced professionals in the field of oncology research, surgical management, and rehabilitation. These two professionals were not members of the five-expert evaluation panel. Case development was informed by current NCCN, ESMO, and CSCO clinical practice guidelines to ensure clinical realism, relevance, and consistency with contemporary standards of care. All cases were designed to reflect real-world multidisciplinary workflows and decision-making pathways, thereby approximating practical clinical and healthcare system contexts and enhancing the relevance of the evaluation for both clinical practice and broader healthcare delivery settings.

### Obtaining responses from LLMs

Figure 1 illustrates the research design framework. To ensure methodological consistency and reproducibility, all three LLMs were evaluated using a standardized prompting strategy. Each model received the same system prompt, “Please act as a professional physician.” A zero-shot prompting approach was adopted; no few-shot examples, reference answers, or additional contextual guidance were provided. Each simulated clinical case was submitted as an independent query in a new conversation session, with chat history reset between cases to prevent contextual carryover and minimize memory bias. Apart from the identical system prompt and case description, no additional prompt engineering or iterative refinement was performed. The complete LLM responses for all simulated cases are provided in Supplementary Material 1, and the standardized prompt template is available in Supplementary Material 2.

All models were accessed through their respective official web interfaces using the default inference settings available at the time of evaluation. No custom temperature, decoding, or other inference parameters were manually adjusted, as these settings were not user-configurable through the web interfaces. Web browsing or external retrieval functions were disabled during testing. This standardized prompting and evaluation protocol ensured that all models were assessed under comparable conditions, thereby improving the reproducibility and fairness of model comparisons.

The generated responses were anonymized, converted into plain text, and stripped of all model-identifying features before evaluation. The order of responses was randomized to maintain assessor blinding. Expert assessment was conducted in three phases separated by 48-hour intervals to minimize potential carryover effects and enhance rating independence.

### Evaluation of LLMs responses

#### Evaluation and scoring of LLM responses

Before formal evaluation, the five multidisciplinary experts participated in a calibration meeting to standardize their understanding of the evaluation criteria and scoring rubric. The assessment framework and scoring principles were developed with reference to current NCCN, ESMO, and CSCO clinical practice guidelines. During the calibration session, the operational definitions of the four evaluation dimensions were reviewed in detail, and representative examples were discussed to ensure that conceptually related dimensions (e.g., accuracy versus relevance) were evaluated independently according to predefined scoring criteria. Because multiple guideline-concordant management strategies may be appropriate for individual lung cancer scenarios, no predefined case-specific “gold standard” answers were established. Instead, each expert independently evaluated each LLM response according to the standardized scoring rubric, considering its consistency with current clinical guidelines, accuracy of clinical reasoning, comprehensiveness, relevance, and clinical applicability.

Anonymised responses from GPT-5.4, Grok 4.1, and DeepSeek-V3.2 (randomly labelled AI1–AI3) were independently double-blind scored by the five experts using a 5-point ordinal Likert scale across four predefined dimensions: accuracy, comprehensiveness, relevance, and applicability. Across all four dimensions, higher scores reflected better performance; specifically, 1 indicated poor performance (e.g., major errors risking harm, critical omissions, largely irrelevant, or unrealistic), whereas 5 indicated excellent performance (e.g., fully guideline-concordant, exhaustive yet concise, perfectly focused, and immediately actionable). Standardized scoring criteria with operational definitions were provided (Supplementary Material 3). Raters were explicitly instructed not to attempt to identify the source model and to base their scores solely on content quality. Final domain-level scores were determined by majority consensus, in cases of no majority (<3 identical scores), the lowest score was conservatively assigned.

### Qualitative analysis of responses from LLM chatbots

Responses identified as potentially misleading or incorrect were further analyzed qualitatively.

### Statistical methods

The study employed R software (version 4.2.2) for statistical analysis and used GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 (GraphPad Software, Inc.) for data visualization and graph plotting.

## Results

### Inter-rater reliability

The Fleiss’ κ statistic demonstrated a statistically significant moderate level of inter-rater agreement among the five raters (κ = 0.463, Z = 17.752, P < 0.05; 95% CI: 0.412–0.514). Sensitivity analysis demonstrated stable reliability: the mean pairwise quadratic-weighted κ was 0.550, and leave-one-rater-out ICC(2, k) ranged from 0.650 to 0.710. The overall ICC (2, k) was 0.675 (95% CI: 0.602–0.745), confirming moderate reliability and a generally consistent, though not identical, pattern of scoring among the experts.

### Performance of GPT, Grok, and DeepSeek in five majors’ clinical domains

Figure 3 illustrates expert ratings across the five evaluated clinical domains. In assessment and diagnosis, as well as treatment decision-making, all LLMs achieved generally high relevance and accuracy, with Grok tending to show more consistent scores and narrower variability across the evaluated cases. DeepSeek tended to receive comparatively lower accuracy ratings in treatment decision-making but relatively higher applicability ratings in prognosis and rehabilitation. In post-operative care and psychosocial support scenarios, all LLMs maintained high relevance and acceptable applicability, while Grok tended to produce more consistent responses across cases. GPT tended to receive intermediate ratings across the evaluated domains. No single LLM consistently outperformed others across all clinical tasks. Given that some clinical domains were represented by only one or two simulated cases, these quantitative observations should be regarded as exploratory and require confirmation in studies with larger and more diverse case sets.
