stem cell self-renewal and differentiation. They proposed that enhancing stem cell “stemness” would amplify differentiation potential under a single culture condition. Using small-molecule modulators of wingless-related integration site (WNT), Notch, and bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) pathways, they optimized intestinal stem cell behavior without artificial gradients. Bromodomain and extraterminal (BET) inhibitors reversibly shifted the balance toward enterocyte differentiation with high proliferation, while niche signal manipulations induced unidirectional differentiation into secretory lineages. The optimized hSIO system yielded organoids with greater cellular diversity (enterocytes, goblet cells, rare Paneth cells) and strong proliferative capacity, overcoming prior limitations by engineering culture conditions rather than post-formation interventions.

Beyond these cornerstone studies, recent efforts have pushed the boundaries of intestinal organoid development through innovative engineering. Zhang et al.36 pioneered a direct reprogramming method using human urine cells to generate intestinal organoids, bypassing the pluripotent stage to reduce tumorigenic risks while preserving structural fidelity to native tissue. Lorenzo-Martín et al.37 introduced a mini-colon model integrating microfabrication and optogenetics, enabling spatiotemporal control of tumorigenesis with organoids exhibiting complex crypt-villus-like patterns. Baghdadi et al.38 explored mechanosensing by knocking out Piezo in mouse organoids, revealing their role in intestinal stem cell self-renewal and differentiation through mechanical cues such as basement membrane stiffness. These studies underscore a trend toward integrating physical constraints, chemical modulators, mechanical cues, or biological tools to refine organoid construction, prioritizing precision and control over traditional self-organization to build robust, reproducible intestinal organoid systems.35

(b)	 Kidney organoids

Kidney organoids are typically derived from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), which differentiate into 3D structures resembling nephron units for studying kidney development and disease. A key aspect of production is mimicking nephron-like structures—proximal and distal tubules, glomeruli, and collecting ducts—with efficiency and scalability. Tran et al.39 achieved a breakthrough by generating thousands of kidney organoids with 1–2 nephron-like structures per unit, using singlecell transcriptomics and immunofluorescence to study nephrogenesis and disease mechanisms. These organoids, patterned through specific signaling pathways, provide insight into processes of human kidney development and disease.

The functional capabilities of kidney organoids, including

filtration and reabsorption, are pivotal for modeling renal diseases. Organoids must replicate processes such as blood filtration and selective reabsorption of water, ions, and nutrients. This has been extensively studied in PKD. In Tran et al.’s39 study, PKD1 and PKD2 mutations induced cyst formation—a hallmark of PKD. Screening 247 protein kinase inhibitors identified compounds that blocked cysts without impairing growth, showing that kidney organoids can recapitulate disease phenotypes and model therapies. Their ability to maintain filtration and reabsorption even in diseased states highlights their value for studying disease progression and testing drugs. Such systems also allow investigation of how nephron dysfunction, as in PKD, alters kidney function.

A major challenge in kidney organoids is achieving sufficient maturation, particularly in the proximal tubule, essential for solute reabsorption. Vanslambrouck et al.’s40 study addresses this by enhancing the specification of metanephric nephron progenitors, producing elongated and functionally distinct proximal tubules. These organoids demonstrated improved functionality, including albumin and organic cation uptake vital for studying nephron reabsorption, better response to the nephrotoxic agent cisplatin, and increased viral replication when exposed to SARS-CoV-2. This maturation of proximal tubules into their S1, S2, and S3 segments allows for more accurate modeling of proximal tubule–related diseases, such as nephrotoxicity and inherited disorders.

In addition to genetic factors, mechanical forces are essential in kidney development. Incorporating physical stress into organoid cultures could improve structure and function, making them more reliable models for kidney disease and regenerative medicine. Prahl et al.’s9 research on nephron-forming niches shows how mechanical stress, generated by mesenchymal cell packing at ureteric bud tips, impacts nephron development. As these niches pack more tightly, they undergo rhythmic stresses that influence cell fate. Mathematical models further demonstrated that kidney curvature constrains this packing, causing a stiffening transition during embryonic development. Such mechanical factors shape the spatial organization of nephron progenitors and their differentiation into podocytes and tubular cells. These insights inform kidney organoid engineering, particularly the design of artificial models that better mimic in vivo tissue behavior (Figure 2b).

Beyond the classic studies of PKD and proximal tubule maturation, efforts to optimize the long-term stability and physiological relevance have contributed to our understanding of kidney organoid functionality, such as studies on the role of specific genes in kidney development. Freedman et al.41 used CRISPR editing to model PKD, confirming the functional defects in PKD1

and PKD2 mutant organoids. Other studies have focused on improving vascularization within kidney organoids to mimic real kidney circulation, essential for filtering blood. Kroll et al.42 developed a perfusable kidney organoid model incorporating endothelial cells to form microcirculation, an essential step toward fully functional organoid systems. These efforts highlight the diverse methodologies used to improve kidney organoid models.

(c)	 Lung organoids

Lung organoids are 3D cell culture models that mimic the structural and functional characteristics of the developing lung in vitro. Their unique morphology and dynamic growth provide insights into lung development and function. The budding growth of lung organoids is a complex process involving differentiation and morphogenesis, driving endoderm induction, foregut patterning, and formation of bronchial and alveolar structures. Notably, lung organoids display highly irregular macroscopic morphologies, reflecting their ability to adapt to the structural and functional features of real lung tissues, making them promising models to study biomechanical strain.

Simulating complex respiratory behaviors—such as dynamic airflow, pressure responses, and biomechanical strain—remains an underexplored aspect of organoid research. Recreating dynamic breathing in lung organoids is key to mimicking physiological function. Some studies have shown bronchial-like cavities within organoids that imitate stretching and contraction, modeling fundamental respiratory processes. Enhancing responses to mechanical strain could support studies of respiratory dynamics in health and disease. Biomechanical strain modeling has also been used to regulate mechanical forces, promoting cellular differentiation and alveolar maturation, and advancing the construction of functional respiratory systems in vitro. Despite individual progress in morphology and function, integrated approaches are needed to optimize the consistency of organoids for structural and functional fidelity. Irregular morphology challenges require highresolution imaging technologies and dynamic monitoring to enhance their modeling accuracy and physiological relevance.

Current protocols for generating lung organoids are time-intensive, requiring optimization to shorten production cycles without compromising biological fidelity. Miller et al.30 introduced a systematic protocol to derive lung organoids from hPSCs, marking a landmark in the field. This multi-step differentiation process mirrors key stages of lung development, including endoderm induction, foregut patterning, and the creation of two organoid types: bud tip progenitor organoids and fetal lung–like organoids. The methodology highlights pathways for improving structural fidelity and cellular characteristics, closely

aligning with human fetal lung tissue while addressing challenges of cellular maturity and functional integration (Figure 2c). The generated lung organoids display bronchial- and bronchiolar-like architectures surrounded by mesenchymal tissue and express alveolar-cell markers, providing a platform to study epithelial–mesenchymal interactions during lung development. Bud tip progenitor organoids contain highly proliferative multipotent cells with multilineage differentiation and strong engraftment potential.

Lung organoids have become indispensable for modeling respiratory diseases and developmental processes. Pezet et al.43 developed a pulmonary fibrosis model using induced respiratory airway progenitors (iRAPs) derived from hPSCs, achieving an unprecedented in vitro replication of fibrosis pathology. Their protocol generated expandable iRAPs closely resembling terminal bronchiolar and alveolar tissues, with a purification rate of ~98%. These iRAPs differentiated into mature alveolar epithelial type I (AT1) and type II (AT2) cells, creating a reliable platform to study disease mechanisms and therapies. By deleting Hermansky– Pudlak syndrome 1 (HPS1) in iRAPs, they reproduced aberrant differentiation features and profibrotic fibroblast recruitment seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This model enabled detailed investigation of respiratory airway/ terminal and respiratory bronchiole (RA/TRB)-associated populations, transitional AT2 cells, and other pathological features of fibrosis. Its scalability allowed production of large quantities of iRAP-derived cells and revealed lineage relationships among airway progenitors, offering insights into fibrosis dynamics unattainable in animal models.

These diverse studies illustrate the versatility and transformative potential of lung organoids in exploring respiratory diseases. Salahudeen et al.44 developed distal lung organoids to study SARS-CoV-2 infection, demonstrating angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor–mediated mechanisms and identifying club cells as infection targets. Leibel et al.45 used lung organoids to examine multi-strain SARS-CoV-2 tropism and pulmonary innate immune responses triggered by canonical and noncanonical viral pathways, uncovering therapeutic opportunities with exogenous surfactants. Important advances have also been made in modeling chronic lung diseases. Basil et al.46 identified respiratory airway secretory cells as progenitors for alveolar AT2 cells, revealing disrupted differentiation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Jones et al.47 examined injury-induced niches and mesenchymal regulation, showing mesenchymal AF1 cells play a critical role in repair outcomes. Furthermore, Budeus et al.31 developed a matrix-free method to generate iPSCderived human lung organoids, providing a robust model to study lung injury, particularly radiation-induced damage, and offering new insights into the radiation sensitivity of

(d)	 Heart organoids

Heart organoids are an important advance in regenerative medicine and cardiac modeling, providing unique insights into early heart development and disease. Among human organoid systems, they have progressed rapidly, particularly in mimicking cardiogenesis and myocardial functions. Their defining feature is the ability to generate beating myocardial tissues—essential for understanding cardiac physiology and clinical applications. Early efforts focused on producing cardiomyocyte aggregates with contractility, while combining biochemical cues, self-organized cellular properties, and engineered scaffolds has since improved their reliability as platforms for modeling structural and cellular heart dynamics. Recent advancements now incorporate chamber formation, epicardial layers, and vascular-like networks. This progression positions heart organoids as key tools for investigating congenital heart defects, cardiomyocyte maturation, and myocardial remodeling. The transition from simple contractility to complex systems with cellular interactions and physiological functions underscores their promise in organ regeneration and therapeutic modeling.

Early heart organoids demonstrated rhythmic contractility and myocardial organization, but newer designs, such as the multilineage self-organized organoid model, mark a significant advance. Branco et al.32 recreated the transient pro-epicardium, a critical feature of cardiac embryogenesis, along with septal transverse mesenchyme and posterior foregut structures. Co-culturing these with cardiomyocyte aggregates produced epicardium– myocardium organoids, which recapitulate epicardial layers covering myocardium-like tissues. This model not only enhances structural fidelity but also reveals interactions between epicardial cells and myocardium, including cardiomyocyte proliferation and maturation driven by paracrine signaling. The development of multilineage organoids underscores the role of morphogen pathways and the necessity of 3D environments to better mimic soluble factor gradients pivotal in cardiac differentiation (Figure 2e).

The primary use of heart organoids is in evaluating therapeutic efficacy for cardiac pathologies, particularly myocardial infarction (MI) repair and cardiovascular toxicity. Yang et al.48 developed an engineered cardiac repair model mimicking MI remodeling. This system captures the phased process—from hypoxic stress and cardiomyocyte apoptosis to fibroblast activation and ECM deposition— while also simulating post-MI electrophysiological dysfunction, a hallmark of cardiac failure. Yang’s approach quantifies cell fate changes and identifies regulatory pathways including transforming growth factor-beta

(TGF-β), Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase (ROCK), and WNT signaling. Validation with modulators such as SB431542 (TGF-β inhibitor) and CHIR99021 (WNT activator) highlights the utility of staged modulation to arrest fibrosis and enhance infarct repair. Beyond functional recovery, the model provides a humanized framework for rapid screening of antifibrotic drugs, though its scope is limited to post-ischemic fibrotic repair. Nonetheless, this engineered model offers a valuable assay platform for drug testing and myocardial regeneration in ischemic heart disease.

As heart organoids advance, their relevance for newborn and adult cardiac pathologies—from myocardial defects to chronic infarction—will deepen. Volmert et al.49 introduced self-organized patterned heart organoids closely resembling human embryogenesis at 6 to 10 weeks of gestation. Their study integrated metabolic and retinoic acid signaling gradients to recapitulate chamber formation and anterior–posterior axis patterning. This model produced functional atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes, organized epicardial structures, and proepicardial organ formation within hollow chambers—features not previously achieved in heart organoids. Demonstrating utility, Kiselev et al.’s system emulated congenital heart defects induced by ondansetron exposure, linking the drug to ventricular septal abnormalities. This model represents a technical advance for pharmacological applications and disease modeling by enabling researchers to trace developmental errors and their outcomes.

Heart organoids are transformative tools in regenerative medicine, providing structural and functional replicas for drug screening and congenital heart defect studies; organoid systems are leveraged for high-throughput screening. Mills et al.10 emphasize how bioengineered cardiac organoids can reduce false-positive hits from 2D assays and provide mechanistic insights into drug efficacy and toxicity, precisely identifying the mevalonate pathway’s central role in cardiomyocyte proliferation. Thus, reliable platforms to study regenerative strategies without compromising organ functionality are needed. Similarly, Zhang et al.’s50 3D cardiac tissue sheet demonstrates enhanced contractility and paracrine cytokine secretion for angiogenesis, facilitating ischemic heart disease studies. Additionally, Lewis et al.’s51

hybrid system integrates 2D and 3D approaches to analyze drug-induced cardiotoxicities, underscoring the versatility of organoids as predictive models. However, immature vascularization, restricted electrophysiological mimicry, and the absence of immune cells and neural crest cells are current limitations.

(e)	 Liver organoids

The liver is a cornerstone of human physiology, orchestrating essential functions such as detoxification and metabolism.

Volume x Issue x (2026) 9  doi: 10.36922/OR026020001

As a parenchymal organ, it depends on hepatocytes—its primary functional cells—to process toxins, metabolize nutrients, and maintain biochemical homeostasis. These hepatocytes are arranged within the liver lobule, a hexagonal unit reflecting the organ’s architectural precision. At the lobule’s periphery, portal triads—composed of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct—deliver a dual blood supply rich in oxygen and nutrients, while the central vein drains processed blood into systemic circulation. This vascular network sustains the liver’s metabolic activity and underscores its role as a detoxifying powerhouse.

Unlike traditional 2D cultures, organoids aim to recapitulate the liver’s 3D complexity, restoring lobular structure and blood supply dynamics to bridge the gap between in vitro models and in vivo reality, with structural fidelity enhancing functional relevance. Tadokoro et al.33 engineered liver organoids to reflect both structural and functional features of the liver, particularly in fibrosis. Starting with human iPSCs (hiPSCs), they developed liver buds—early fetal liver–like structures—and fused them into larger liver organoids mimicking midgestational fetal liver. This fusion fostered interactions among hepatocytes, endothelial cells, and mesenchymal cells, producing complex structures with hepatocytes, vasculature, and bile ducts after transplantation. The goal was not to replicate adult liver anatomy but to harness fetal liver’s regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. When grafted onto chemically induced fibrotic livers in immunocompromised mice, these hiPSC-derived liver organoids integrated with host vasculature and promoted regeneration. A key feature was their ability to reduce fibrosis via M2 macrophage polarization, driven by secretion of macrophage-recruiting and antifibrotic factors—more pronounced in fetal than adult liver. This design leveraged fetal-specific traits such as hematopoiesis to influence the host microenvironment (Figure 2f).

A pragmatic compromise is to sacrifice some anatomical detail for high-throughput analysis. Kimura et al.7 took a distinct yet complementary approach that emphasizes metabolic fidelity, restoring sufficient hepatocyte function to study genetic impacts and probe genotype–phenotype associations in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) without prioritizing complex structures such as bile ducts or sinusoids. His team devised a pooled human organoid panel from hiPSC-derived hepatocytes, engineered to emulate steatohepatitis under insulin-insensitive conditions—a reflection of the liver’s metabolic role in diabetic states. These organoids were not designed to replicate full lobular architecture but to provide a scalable platform for largescale phenotyping, focusing on lipid accumulation and inflammation as NASH hallmarks. A key finding was the role of the GCKR-rs1260326:C>T variant, which modulates disease severity depending on metabolic context. Their

method differentiated foregut progenitors into hepatic organoids, maintaining hepatocyte identity while exposing them to fatty acid overload to mimic NASH pathology. This setup enabled identification of mitochondrial dysfunction linked to the GCKR variant, critical for drug evaluation and disease modeling.

A challenge in liver organoid design is prevascularization without compromising parenchymal integrity. Fan et al.52 introduced a nonparenchymal cell grafting strategy to construct hiPSC-derived hepatobiliary organoids (hHBOs) by integrating endothelial and mesenchymal cells at defined differentiation stages. The process began with foregut stem cell spheroids differentiated into hHBOs on a microfabricated chip, avoiding Matrigel for uniformity. Endothelial grafting was optimized at the hepatic maturation stage, when hepatocytes expressed vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiopoietins, promoting endothelial invasion and sprouting to mimic sinusoidal development. Mesenchymal cells, notably MRC-5 fibroblasts, enhanced this process, stabilizing vasculature and modestly boosting lipid metabolism via ASGR1 upregulation, without altering hepatocyte fate. Post-transplantation into mice, these prevascularized hHBOs integrated with host vasculature and self-organized into hepatic zones and bile ducts, reflecting the liver lobule’s dual blood supply and biliary network.

Beyond these flagship studies, many efforts have enriched liver organoid development, each addressing structural and functional restoration. Leite et al.53 crafted 3D spheroids combining HepaRG hepatocytes and primary human hepatic stellate cells to detect drug-induced fibrosis by maintaining hepatic stellate cell quiescence alongside hepatocyte metabolic competence. This model, responsive to compounds such as allyl alcohol and methotrexate, mirrors the liver’s injury-response dynamics without its full lobular architecture. Wu et al.54 scaled up hepatic precursor organoids using human ESCs in bioreactors, embedding low-concentration Matrigel to support expansion while retaining hepatocyte polarity—ideal for drug testing despite heterogeneity risks. Liu et al.55 fabricated decellularized liver scaffolds seeded with hiPSC-derived cells with restored organ-level vasculature and metabolism, prioritizing sinusoidal-like structures for toxicity studies. Wang et al.56 demonstrated that hepatobiliary organoids incorporated functional bile ducts, leveraging polarized hepatocytes to study clearance functions. Utami et al.57 used oxygen-permeable microwells to enhance cytochrome P450 (CYP) activity, refining drug metabolism models. These approaches emphasize restoring key liver features— vascularity, biliary networks, or metabolic zones—tailored to fatty liver and fibrosis modeling; they share a focus on structural ingenuity over experimental minutiae.

### 2.1.3. Brain and nerve organoids

Brain organoids represent a major advance in modeling the human nervous system, bridging the gap between simplistic cell cultures and the complexity of in vivo studies.59 Derived from iPSCs, these 3D constructs can self-organize into structures mimicking the whole brain or specific regions— forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, and thalamus. Qian et al.58 developed a miniaturized spinning bioreactor system, SpinΩ, to generate human brain organoids with greater reproducibility and lower cost. Using this system, they cultured forebrain-specific organoids from hiPSCs that displayed key features of human cortical development, including a well-organized outer subventricular zone with

neural progenitor cells and organized neuronal subtypes across all six cortical layers. These forebrain organoids also produced γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neurons, reflecting features unique to human brain development and absent in rodent models. The versatility of SpinΩ was further demonstrated in generating midbrain and hypothalamic organoids. The forebrain platform was applied to model Zika virus (ZIKV) infection, showing that African and Asian ZIKV strains preferentially infect neural progenitors, causing increased cell death and suppressed proliferation. This reduced neuronal layer volume, resembling the pathological features of human microcephaly. The ability to model ZIKV infection at different stages of cortical

Son et al.59 also presented a 3D-engineered brain–spinal cord assembloid on a multielectrode array (MEA) chip to geometrically align these components with signal transmission across the central–peripheral divide. Assembloids are spatially organized multicellular constructs and organoids that function more like real human tissue and organs produced from diverse cell types (Figure 3b).

Cortical organoids, for example, can differentiate into all brain regions, offering a panoramic view of neurogenesis. Electrophysiological recordings and calcium imaging further demonstrated neuronal maturation and network activity in fused organoids. Xiang et al.60 presented a method for generating region-specific brain organoids with features of the medullary spinal trigeminal nuclei (SpV). Using hPSCs with small mothers against decapentaplegic (SMAD) inhibition and WNT/RA activation, they created SpV-like organoids (hmSpVOs) that exhibited morphological and molecular characteristics of the medullary SpV, including lineage markers and neural connectivity with the thalamus. By integrating hmSpVOs with thalamic organoids, they established a functional SpV–thalamus circuit. Another study explored reciprocal projection loops by fusing human ESC–derived thalamic-like organoids (hThOs)

with cortical-like organoids, offering new ways to study thalamocortical interactions. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that hThOs uniquely expressed thalamic markers, with glutamatergic neurons predominating. When fused with human cortical–like organoids, hThOs extended axons forming thalamocortical projections, while cortical neurons projected back to the thalamus, establishing corticothalamic connections. Immunostaining confirmed synapse formation, mimicking in vivo thalamocortical pathways (Figure 3c).

Beyond these milestones, numerous studies enrich the neurosystem organoid landscape. Region-specific organoids, such as those of the spinal cord or fused assemblies (e.g., cortex–optic nerve), allow targeted exploration of functional specialization. Yin et al.61 reported a significant advancement in human neuromusculoskeletal tri-tissue organoids (hNMSOs) with their integration of neural, muscular, and skeletal domains within a single 3D construct. Starting from hiPSCs, they employed a static-tospinning co-development strategy, using Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling and skeletogenic factors to induce simultaneous lineage differentiation. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptome profiling confirmed distinct lineages and their spatial organization in hNMSOs. The neural domain acquired a ventral-specific identity and generated motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscles. These organoids self-organized into spatially distinct yet interconnected regions—neural zones with ventral motor neurons, contractile muscle, and supportive skeletal tissue. During the maturation process of hNMSOs, the three tissues showed tissue-specific development (Figure 3d). Functional studies demonstrate that hNMSOs have robust spontaneous electrical activity with functional connections between neural and muscular tissues, motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle, and skeletal support enhancing muscle maturation. Moreover, hNMSOs provide a valuable model for studying human neuromusculoskeletal crosstalk and related diseases.

### 2.1.4. Vascularized organoids

The development of vascularized organoids marks a pivotal step in overcoming one of organoid technology’s main challenges: establishing a functional vascular network. iPSC-derived organoids are particularly promising due to their pluripotency and ability to differentiate into endothelial cells and mural cells, including pericytes and vascular smooth muscle cells. Without robust vasculature, organoids suffer from limited nutrient and oxygen delivery, often leading to necrosis in larger constructs. Advances in this field highlight the potential of iPSC-derived vascularized organoids to bridge in vitro and in vivo physiology, offering insights into vascular development and tissue engineering.


<!-- Page 12 -->


Volume x Issue x (2026) 12  doi: 10.36922/OR026020001

Vascularization not only supports cell survival but also enhances physiological relevance by mimicking in vivo tissue dynamics, critical for disease modeling and regenerative medicine. A landmark study by Du et al.62 exemplifies engineering approaches to vascularize organoids through a patient-derived tumor organoid (PDTO)-on-a-chip model. This system integrates PDTOs with microfluidic technology to construct a hierarchical, tumor-specific microvascular network, reflecting the structural diversity of clinical tumors. PDTOs were seeded within a multi-channel microfluidic chip alongside endothelial cells, enabling self-assembled vasculature with perfusable lumens and tumor-induced angiogenic sprouting. The model produced a layered architecture, with disorganized angiogenesis near the tumor and organized microvessels distally, closely mimicking in vivo tumor vasculature. Microfluidics provided precise microenvironmental control, facilitating nutrient supply and real-time monitoring of tumor–vascular dynamics. This platform prioritized vascular functionality—ensuring perfusion and structural integrity—rather than focusing only on downstream applications. While the study highlighted Notch signaling in tumor cell migration toward vessels, its key contribution was demonstrating a scalable, reproducible method for vascularizing heterogeneous organoids. Particularly relevant for vascular-rich tumors such as sarcomas, this model sets a precedent for strategies emphasizing vascular fidelity and adaptability, offering a versatile tool for studying vascularization across organoid types (Figure 3e).

The process typically begins with mesoderm induction of iPSC aggregates, followed by endothelial differentiation within a 3D matrix such as collagen I–Matrigel to form vessel-like structures. In contrast to engineered systems, Wimmer et al.65 developed a protocol for generating self-organizing 3D blood vessel organoids from hPSCs, emphasizing intrinsic cellular mechanisms over external manipulation. The process begins with mesoderm induction of hPSC aggregates, followed by differentiation into endothelial networks and pericytes within a collagen I– Matrigel matrix, yielding organoids that recapitulate human microvasculature within 2–3 weeks. The vascular networks feature endothelial cell–lined vessels supported by mural cells, forming a scalable system expandable in suspension culture. A key feature is integration with host vasculature upon transplantation into immunocompromised mice, where organoids matured into functional arteries, arterioles, and veins connected to mouse circulation. This self-assembly leverages the developmental potential of hPSCs, bypassing biofabrication tools such as bioprinting yet achieving a perfusable vascular system. The focus is on construction—optimizing differentiation cues and matrix composition—rather than post-formation analyses, making

it a foundational technique for vascularizing organoids such as brain or liver models. While lacking active flow in vitro, its transplantability suggests a path toward functional perfusion, offering a complementary strategy to engineered approaches and underscoring the versatility of hPSCderived systems in vascular organoid research.

This self-organizing capacity enables hierarchical vascular networks resembling native microvasculature, forming the basis for functional organoids. Another approach to vascularization involves co-culturing vascular and organ-specific organoids, as in the development of vascularized brain organoids. In this strategy, vascular organoids are fused with brain organoids, cultivating endothelial and neural lineages together to form blood– brain barrier (BBB)-like structures. Vascular organoids rich in endothelial cells are embedded with brain organoids in a supportive matrix, allowing spontaneous vascular branching and integration with neural tissue. The resulting vascularized brain organoids show selective permeability characteristic of the BBB, supported by microglial cells that enhance functionality through immune responses and synapse phagocytosis. Unlike bioprinted or microfluidic systems, this method relies on cellular self-organization, augmented by cues such as VEGF to promote endothelial differentiation and vessel formation. The study emphasized construction over experimental outcomes, focusing on building a robust vascular network that supports neurogenesis without requiring active perfusion in vitro.66

While diverse in execution, they share a focus on constructing functional vasculature, with variations in complexity and scalability suited to different organoid applications. Achieving a perfusable, stable vascular system remains a technical hurdle, requiring innovative engineering strategies. Beyond these examples, several studies have advanced vascularization strategies with distinct methods. Liu et al.67 used genetic engineering by introducing an inducible ETS variant transcription factor 2 (ETV2) into kidney organoids, achieving robust endothelialization that enhanced nephron maturation without external scaffolds. Skylar-Scott et al.68 utilized orthogonal differentiation of stem cells to co-develop vascular and neural lineages in cortical organoids, generating spatially organized vascular networks via cell aggregation. Holloway et al.69 optimized culture conditions to maintain endogenous endothelial cells in intestinal organoids, resulting in vascularized constructs with organ-specific identity through intrinsic mechanisms. Additionally, 3D bioprinting has emerged as a powerful engineering tool, with applications in liver and breast tumor organoids, where precise deposition of endothelial cells and biomaterials forms perfusable vascular channels. These approaches illustrate techniques ranging from selfassembly to bioengineering that address the challenge of vascularizing organoids.70

### 2.1.5. Tumor organoids

Patient-derived tumor organoids preserve important histological and genetic features of their source tumors, but conventional expansion can be too slow and materialintensive for clinical drug selection. Hu et al.34 addressed this limitation by coupling lung cancer organoids with an integrated superhydrophobic microwell array chip (InSMAR-chip). As shown in Figure 2g, the device contains 108 microwells of approximately 440 nL each, allowing passage-0 organoids to be distributed into isolated 3D cultures and exposed to multiple drugs without prolonged expansion. The miniaturized workflow generated drug-response results within one week while maintaining organoid growth, viability, and parentaltumor characteristics. Agreement with genomic alterations, xenograft responses, and available clinical outcomes illustrates how microengineering can convert organoid heterogeneity from a practical barrier into a rapid, patientspecific testing opportunity.

Despite varied origins, their shared strength is recapitulating tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental features, laying a foundation for downstream studies. Papargyriou et al.71 developed a branched organoid model for PDAC, embedded in collagen gels, that effectively recapitulated the phenotypic diversity and heterogeneity observed in vivo. Derived from patient tumor tissues, these organoids exhibited morphologies linked to transcriptional programs such as EMT, reflecting PDAC subtypes and cellular states. The study showed that organoids captured both intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity, with epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes displaying distinct responses to chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Using Morphologic Organoid Phenotypic Heterogeneity Mapping (MOrPHeMap), the authors quantified this diversity and identified phenotype-specific therapeutic targets, such as mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase/ rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma (MEK/RAF) inhibitors that reprogrammed mesenchymal organoids into a uniform phenotype. This finding highlights PDAC’s notorious drug resistance, potentially driven by phenotypic plasticity, with organoids providing a platform to dissect these mechanisms. Unlike mutation-driven models, this approach emphasizes dynamic phenotypic changes, underscoring organoids’ superiority in simulating complex disease progression. Nonetheless, the model’s limited microenvironmental representation suggests the need for immune cell co-cultures to enhance clinical relevance.

Compared to 2D cell lines, their 3D structure more closely mimics in vivo conditions, reducing genetic drift from prolonged passaging. Glioma organoids from samples often pose challenges in tissue acquisition and culture. Peng et al.72 proposed an individualized patient tumor organoid (IPTO) model for central nervous system

tumors, including glioma, by culturing patient-derived tumor explants in iPSC-derived cerebral organoids. Within 10 days, IPTOs were generated with a higher success rate than traditional methods. Validated through histopathology, genomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing, IPTOs preserved cellular heterogeneity, molecular features, and the microenvironment of parental tumors, accurately predicting patient responses to chemotherapy (e.g., temozolomide) and targeted therapies, including resistance mechanisms. IPTOs avoid dissociation-induced spatial heterogeneity, combine rapid establishment with microenvironment retention, and are particularly suited for diverse central nervous system tumors, especially given glioma’s invasive nature.

Tumor organoids share key features: high-throughput cultivation, pronounced heterogeneity, and close resemblance to parental tumors. These attributes make them pivotal for drug screening, disease mechanism studies, organoid biobanks, and bioinformaticsassisted drug development. Rao et al.73 established liver cancer organoids with a 40.9% success rate, tailoring chemotherapy for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma via drug sensitivity testing. Jia et al.74 used single-cell transcriptomics to reveal molecular subtype heterogeneity in breast cancer organoids, with implications for lung cancer. Xu et al.75 developed a high-throughput screening platform, identifying seven drug candidates in cervical cancer organoids, showcasing efficiency applicable to drug development. Mo et al.76 constructed a colorectal cancer liver metastasis organoid biobank, capturing heterogeneity and predicting chemotherapy responses to liver cancer. Liu et al.77 paired lung cancer organoids with single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect immunotherapy responses in the microenvironment. Across cancer types, these studies underscore organoids’ high-throughput and heterogeneity advantages. They signal a shift from isolated models to integrated platforms, particularly for bioinformaticsaided drug development, though success rates and microenvironment simulation remain challenges requiring interdisciplinary solutions.

### 2.2. Organ-on-a-chip and human multi-organ-on-achip systems

Organ-on-a-chip platforms are microfluidic systems that use micro- and nanoscale fabrication and controlled fluid flow to emulate selected human-organ functions in vitro.1,78 Depending on scope, OoC platforms can be classified as single-organ devices or multi-organ systems. Single-organ devices reproduce selected liver, kidney, gut, or cardiac functions using organ-specific microarchitectures.79 Multi-organ systems connect distinct tissue modules to model inter-organ communication, systemic responses, and pharmacokinetic (PK)–pharmacodynamic (PD)

interactions, including drug–drug interactions.80,81

Common configurations include single-layer channels for simple organ models, double-layer channels for barrier tissues (e.g., BBB), and hydrogel-channel types for mimicking ECM environments.82 The transition from single-organ to multi-organ OoCs requires careful engineering of features such as vascular systems, nutrient gradients, and dynamic fluid communication to ensure proper functional interdependence.83 Closed-chamber multi-organ systems minimize dead volumes for stable

perfusion but limit accessibility, whereas open-access systems allow manual interaction with cultures but suffer from dead volume constraints.82,84 Although their clinical use faces challenges such as scalability, standardization, and inter-model validation,83 they could provide better cost-effective systems for predictive toxicology, disease modeling, and pharmaceutical development.79 Innovations such as incorporating microfluidic-controlled perfusion, artificial intelligence (AI) for real-time monitoring, and advanced imaging technologies have improved the precision and reproducibility of OoCs.78,85

### 2.2.1. Single-organ-on-a-chip

(a)	 Lung organ-on-a-chip

Lung-on-a-chip technology reproduces key structural and physiological features of the human alveolar–capillary interface. It enables dynamic interactions between alveolar epithelium and vascular endothelium under air–liquid interface conditions and can incorporate cyclic strain to mimic breathing. These controlled mechanical and fluidic cues support studies of gas exchange, inflammation, infection, inhalation toxicity, and therapeutic response.91 Combining an air–liquid interface with mechanical actuation therefore makes lung-on-a-chip a useful model of both pulmonary physiology and disease.

One of the earliest breakthroughs in lung-on-a-chip came from Huh et al.11 in 2010, presenting a biomimetic microsystem that replicated the human alveolar– capillary interface, the critical unit for gas exchange. Using microfabrication, the team created a microfluidic device with a porous, flexible membrane separating two microchannels. Human alveolar epithelial and pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells were cultured on opposite sides, forming functional monolayers. Cyclic strain applied to the membrane mimicked alveolar stretching during breathing. The system enabled studies of biological responses to stimuli such as bacterial infection and inflammation. It also simulated infection responses, showing neutrophil migration and engulfment of Escherichia coli on the epithelial surface. Mechanical strain was further shown to enhance inflammatory and toxic responses of lung cells to silica nanoparticles, a common inhalation toxicity model (Figure 4a).

Mimicking the spherical geometry of the cell’s natural microenvironment improves the physiological fidelity of cell culture based on a biomimetic morphology of a 3D respiratory epithelial tissue structure.92,93 Huang et al.94 introduced a biomimetic alveolar lung-on-a-chip model that replicates the 3D structure and physiological functions of human pulmonary alveoli. Notably, a 3D porous hydrogel made of gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) with an inverse opal structure, which mimics the sac-like pores and interconnecting windows of alveolar sacs, was used. The GelMA scaffold, fabricated using sacrificial alginate microbeads, features uniform, interconnected pores with a stiffness (~6.23 kPa) similar to that of native lung tissue, providing a physiologically relevant microenvironment for cell growth. This structure supports the formation of a functional epithelial monolayer when seeded with primary human alveolar epithelial cells, which exhibit high viability and form tight junctions, essential for alveolar barrier function. The model is integrated into a poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) chip that simulates cyclic breathing motions through mechanical actuation, applying

8% strain to mimic physiological alveolar expansion. This dynamic environment promotes cell spreading, proliferation, and the maintenance of in vivo-like behaviors.

More recent innovations range from viral infections and cancer therapeutics to inflammatory and fibrotic diseases.95 Si et al.96 developed a human airway-on-a-chip platform lined with bronchial epithelia to study viral infection dynamics and drug efficacy. In an influenza A–infected airway-on-a-chip, nafamostat co-administered with oseltamivir extended the treatment window. Moreover, amodiaquine was identified as an effective therapeutic for SARS-CoV-2 infection, demonstrating the platform’s potential for antiviral screening. Deinhardt-Emmer et al.97 used a human alveolus-on-a-chip to show that secondary Staphylococcus aureus infection after influenza damages the endothelial barrier. Building on this, Zhang et al.98 utilized a similar alveolar-on-a-chip to replicate SARS- CoV-2-induced lung injury, showing that epithelial cells were more susceptible to viral infection than endothelial cells. The addition of immune cells allowed the targeted viral infection model to recapitulate immune infiltration and inflammatory cytokine release, with remdesivir treatment mitigating barrier disruption and viral replication.

Lung-on-a-chip systems are recreating human-relevant respiratory physiology and responses, with vascular integration offering insights into endothelial damage and immune-cell interactions. Thacker et al.99 used a vascularized lung-on-a-chip to show how SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers endotheliitis and persistent inflammatory responses marked by interleukin 6 (IL-6) secretion; tocilizumab reduced but did not fully prevent barrier loss. Dasgupta et al.100 modeled acute radiation–induced lung injury and reproduced DNA damage, inflammatory cytokine upregulation, and barrier dysfunction, enabling tests of lovastatin and prednisolone. More recently, Ringquist et al.101 developed an immune-competent lungon-a-chip that reproduced major features of the human severe-influenza response, providing an appropriate infection-model context for the previously uncited study.

(b)	 Gut organ-on-a-chip

Gut-on-a-chip (GoC) technology represents a major advance in in vitro modeling of the human intestine, aiming to replicate its physiological, mechanical, and biochemical dynamics. The intestine is essential for nutrient absorption, barrier function, microbiota interactions, and drug metabolism. GoC studies highlight the importance of dynamic flow for maintaining constant shear stress during cell differentiation, enhancing polarization and tight junction formation with crypt-villus-like structures.102 Guo et al.103 developed a single-layer GoC model using Caco-2 cells cultured under dynamic shear flow with a porous membrane and ECM support. This enabled formation of

a highly polarized, compact monolayer expressing tight junction proteins and elevated differentiation markers such as villin and sucrase–isomaltase. Compared to static systems, this model greatly improved drug metabolism studies related to nutrient absorption and barrier function.

Conventional models such as 2D cultures or animal systems often fail to capture its structural, cellular, and functional complexity. Beyond single-layer designs, double-layer GoC systems enhance physiological relevance by separating luminal and vascular compartments. Grassart et al.102 used such a platform to study Shigella infection, revealing how mechanical forces such as flow and peristalsis enhance bacterial invasion by leveraging the microenvironment, including crypt-like epithelial structures. Shim et al.104 incorporated villi-like 3D collagen scaffolds into a double-layer device, achieving improved gut barrier function and enzymatic activity under fluidic shear stress. Jing et al.105 further demonstrated a gut-vessel microfluidic system where intestinal epithelial cells were co-cultured with vascular endothelial cells under peristaltic motion, resulting in functional microvilli, glycocalyx layer formation, and successful bacterial co-culture.

Gut-on-a-chip has provided new insights into microbiome-mediated intestinal inflammation, serving as a platform for modeling intestinal diseases and testing therapeutic interventions. Kim et al.87 presented a GoC model incorporating microbiome, immune cells, and mechanical deformation to explore bacterial overgrowth and inflammation. The model mimics human intestinal pathophysiology, enabling long-term in vitro culture of epithelium, immune cells, and commensal microbes— crucial for studying diseases such as ileus and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The study showed that mechanical deformation is essential for intestinal health, as the absence of peristalsis-like motion led to bacterial overgrowth resembling IBD and ileus. It also revealed that immune cell interactions with endotoxins or non-pathogenic microbes stimulated proinflammatory cytokine production, contributing to epithelial injury and barrier dysfunction, key to understanding the inflammatory processes driving these diseases (Figure 4b).

Gut-on-a-chip platforms address limitations by simulating fluid flow, peristalsis, and oxygen gradients through microfluidics. Advances in GoC technology have facilitated the study of intestinal microbiome interactions, supported by oxygen gradients and mechanical forces, enabling insights into gut physiology and drug effects.106,107 Ballerini et al.86 developed a GoC model that simulates the human intestinal environment, incorporating human fecal microbiota and peristaltic-like movements to investigate microbiome–host interactions and predict responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma patients. By integrating human intestinal organoids, microvascular

endothelial cells, and patient-derived fecal samples, the system supported multiomic analysis, revealing epitheliumspecific biomarkers and microbial factors linked to clinical outcomes. The findings indicated that the microbiome of non-responders to immune checkpoint inhibitors had reduced capacity to buffer cellular stress and selfrenew, while specific microbial and soluble components correlated with clinical features. This GoC platform not only recapitulates microbiome–host interactions but also provides insights into molecular mechanisms influencing therapeutic responses, enabling identification of prognostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets.

Gut-on-a-chip devices have also been applied to model intestinal diseases and screen therapies. Wu et al.108 developed an intestine-on-a-chip integrated with machine learning to screen probiotics for enteritis relief, identifying Bifidobacterium longum as the most effective strain for reducing inflammation and enhancing epithelial integrity. Shin et al.109 reported a patient-derived intestinal organoid–based device that recapitulates disease-specific differentiation patterns under dynamic biomechanical conditions, demonstrating its potential for personalized disease modeling, including Crohn’s disease and colorectal cancer. While GoC platforms provide improved physiological relevance compared to traditional models, challenges remain in standardization and scalability for high-throughput applications. Donkers et al.110 highlighted the broad design variability in GoC systems and underscored the need for integrated approaches to optimize preclinical drug development and disease modeling. Özkan et al.111 emphasized the potential of GoC systems in personalized medicine, particularly for understanding gut microbiota interactions, disease mechanisms, and testing therapeutic interventions.

(c)	 Liver organ-on-a-chip

Liver-on-a-chip platforms combine controlled perfusion with multicellular 3D culture to reproduce key aspects of hepatic transport, metabolism, and vascular organization. Photocontrolled porous scaffolds and co-cultures with endothelial and stromal cells have improved albumin secretion, urea synthesis, CYP expression, and the stability of long-term hepatotoxicity models.112,113 Li et al.88 further developed a microneedle-assisted hepatic acinus chip (Figure 4c). Its acinus-inspired culture region connected portal-vein, hepatic-artery, and central-vein pathways through microneedle-generated sinusoid-like channels with radii of 100–200 µm. The three inlet streams were operated at 2, 1, and 1 mL/min, respectively, and the perfusable microsystem remained stable during 7–14 days of culture. This design improved intratissue flow, cell viability, microstructure formation, and hepatic metabolic function, while also showing that channel dimensions and flow partitioning must be reported when liver-on-a-chip

performance is compared across platforms.

The liver, a highly vascularized organ, makes in vitro modeling challenging. Vascularization is essential for improving the biological accuracy of liver-on-a-chip systems, together with its complexity—arising from diverse cell types including hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, hepatic stellate cells, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells. To address this, Ya et al.114 developed a liver lobule-on-a-chip with self-assembled, perfusable hepatic sinusoid networks using microfluidic-guided angiogenesis, resulting in higher metabolic activity and prolonged hepatocyte function. Lee et al.115 created an implantable vascularized liver-ona-chip that supported liver bud maintenance and modeled inflammatory and fibrotic progression during NAFLD. This model proved predictive in in vitro and in vivo studies. For hepatocellular carcinoma, Özkan et al.116 engineered a vascularized hepatocellular carcinoma-on-a-chip system, incorporating tunable collagen matrices and liver-specific cells to analyze chemoresistance and treatment efficacy under physiologically relevant conditions. Matsumoto et al.117 further replicated hepatic zonation by employing oxygen gradients in microfluidic devices to simulate zonal liver functions, including xenobiotic metabolism and carbohydrate processing.

The liver, a metabolically active organ, is central to drug detoxification, nutrient metabolism, and immune response. Liver-on-a-chip systems effectively model liver diseases and evaluate potential therapies. Chhabra et al.’s118 shear device enabled the modulation of cytokine environments to regulate endothelial–hepatocyte interactions, facilitating studies on regenerative responses. Nawroth et al.119 designed a triculture liver-on-a-chip to study alcohol-associated liver disease, recapitulating key markers such as lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and bile canaliculi remodeling under ethanol exposure, with potential for patient-specific research. These platforms have also advanced studies on liver regeneration and drug-induced liver injury (DILI). For DILI research, Hou et al.120 developed a stacked array on a chip to investigate idiosyncratic DILI mechanisms, identifying cytokinedriven macrophage polarization as a critical factor. Such models enhance our understanding of drug toxicity and liver repair mechanisms.

(d)	 Heart organ-on-a-chip

Heart-on-a-chip (HoC) technology integrates humanrelevant cardiac tissue engineering and microfluidics to model cardiac physiology and pathology. It bridges the gap between simplistic cell cultures and the physiological complexity of the human heart, replicating myocardial structure and function, and is invaluable for studying cardiovascular diseases, a leading cause of mortality worldwide. HoC platforms have shown versatility in

recapitulating cardiac microenvironments. Zhao et al.121 engineered chamber-specific cardiac microtissues from hiPSCs, creating atrial- and ventricular-specific tissues with distinct drug responses and electrical conductivity. This platform also facilitated long-term modeling of diseases such as left ventricular hypertrophy and targeted drug testing and disease-specific modeling. Similarly, Veldhuizen et al.122 advanced HoC by co-culturing hPSC-derived cardiomyocytes with cardiac fibroblasts in a microfluidic platform that provided controllable microenvironments. This biomimetic approach, incorporating anisotropic architecture, enhanced tissue maturation and synchronous contractions, closely mimicking native myocardium.

Genetic and patient-specific disease models have further expanded HoC capabilities. Park et al.123 developed an optogenetic HoC model to study catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, a genetically driven arrhythmia. Using precise genetic editing, the system reproduced hallmark events such as diastolic Ca2+ waves and reentrant rhythms, enabling identification of molecular mechanisms, including the role of ryanodine receptor phosphorylation in arrhythmogenesis. For ischemic heart disease, Gaballah et al.124 established a hypoxic HoC model using hPSC-derived cardiomyocytes to study oxygen deprivation. The system demonstrated hypoxia-induced arrhythmias, sarcomere disorganization, and impaired Ca2+ handling. The therapeutic potential of the antiarrhythmic drug levosimendan was observed, as it mitigated arrhythmias and preserved sarcomere integrity under hypoxic stress, positioning HoC as a preclinical tool for ischemic heart disease studies. Liu et al.125 complemented this work by integrating bioelectronics into a HoC model for real-time monitoring of cardiac electrophysiology. This platform revealed hypoxia-induced tachycardia and arrhythmias, provided insights into ionchannel behavior during acute hypoxia, and enabled detailed electrophysiological analyses.

Heart-on-a-chip platforms typically combine microfluidic chip fabrication with engineered cardiac microtissues, mimicking key aspects of human MPS while providing controllable microenvironments and real-time feedback. Microfluidic systems have advanced 3D cardiac tissue modeling, improving physiological relevance. Chen et al.126 reviewed innovations in HoC technology, highlighting progress in microfluidic chip fabrication and real-time feedback systems. These 3D microtissues show superior mechanical and electrical properties compared to monolayer cultures, providing a reliable platform for modeling cardiac responses to drugs and environmental stimuli. Wu et al.127 further emphasized integrating HoC with blood vessel-on-a-chip systems, enabling studies of cardiac–vascular interactions. This approach is especially valuable for investigating cardiovascular

disease mechanisms and supporting high-throughput drug screening.

Hence, HoC platforms provide physiologically relevant models for studying cardiac biology, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic interventions. Their ability to integrate patient-derived cells, replicate tissue-specific responses, and enable real-time monitoring underscores the versatility and clinical potential of HoC technology in cardiovascular research and personalized medicine. Despite progress, challenges remain in fabricating scalable, high-throughput HoC systems that replicate complex cardiac physiology, including large vessels and valves. Recent innovations such as bilayer membrane microfluidic devices and vascularized networks for tissue perfusion offer promising solutions by improving oxygen and nutrient delivery to cardiac tissues.126 These systems refine the in vitro microenvironment and enhance HoC functionality for pharmaceutical research. Agarwal et al.89 presented a high-throughput HoC system using semi-automated fabrication to create submillimeter thin-film cantilevers from soft elastomers. Engineered with anisotropic cardiac microtissues mimicking ventricular laminar architecture, these cantilevers allow calculation of systolic and diastolic stresses from deflection during contraction. The microdevice, made from autoclavable materials, ensures reusability and compatibility with optical and electrical assays for cardiac contractility. Its ability to test drug effects, such as isoproterenol, is enhanced by scalability and reproducibility, making it a promising tool for pharmacological studies, particularly with rare or expensive cell sources (Figure 4d).

(e)	 Kidney organ-on-a-chip

The development of kidney OoC systems represents a promising innovation in biomedical engineering, providing dynamic in vitro models to mimic the complex structure and functions of the human kidney, especially the glomerulus. This platform offers a robust tool for studying glomerular diseases, drug screening, and personalized medicine, providing insights into kidney disorder mechanisms and possible interventions.128 These devices integrate human cells within microfluidic environments to reproduce tissue morphology, organ-level function, and disease phenotypes. Kidney OoC systems often use microfluidic platforms to recreate the kidney’s dynamic environment. Musah et al.90 developed a glomerulus-on-a-chip (GOAC) made of flexible PDMS with two parallel microchannels separated by a porous PDMS membrane (Figure 4e). This structure mimics the tissue–tissue interface of the glomerular capillary wall. HiPSC-derived intermediate mesoderm cells were cultured in the top channel and differentiated into podocytes in situ, while primary human glomerular microvascular endothelial cells were seeded on the opposite side. Cyclic suction applied to hollow chambers flanking the channels mimicked the stretching and relaxation of living

glomeruli. The chip reproduced the differential molecular filtration of the glomerular wall, retaining albumin in the vasculature while allowing inulin to pass into the urinary space. These features make the GOAC a powerful tool for studying renal mechanisms and diseases.

Recent advances have enabled the recreation of kidney filtration processes, critical for understanding renal physiology and pathophysiology. A key feature of kidney OoCs is their ability to replicate renal filtration, selectively handling small molecules such as urea and creatinine while retaining macromolecules such as albumin. Petrosyan et al.129 presented a GOAC model that mimics the human glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) using human podocytes and glomerular endothelial cells in a microfluidic platform. Unlike models with artificial membranes, this GOAC allows direct podocyte–endothelial interaction, essential for reproducing native GFB structure and function. The chip’s three-channel system co-cultures human podocytes and glomerular endothelial cells on a collagen I matrix, enabling formation of a functional GFB with ECM components such as collagen IV and laminin. The GOAC shows selective permeability, filtering inulin while retaining albumin, similar to in vivo function. It also responds to pathological conditions, including hyperglycemia, nephrotoxic agents such as puromycin aminonucleoside, and sera from membranous nephropathy patients, with albumin leakage proportional to clinical proteinuria levels.

Simulating filtration and blood purification holds strong potential for advancing knowledge of kidney diseases and therapeutic strategies. A major advantage of kidney OoC systems is their potential for disease modeling. Mou et al.130 designed a device incorporating a biomimetic ultrathin membrane made from electrospun silk fibroin to establish an epithelial–endothelial interface. This platform supports differentiation of hiPSCs into glomerular cells, including podocytes and endothelial cells, essential for forming the kidney’s filtration barrier. Integration of these cells enabled the development of a functional GOAC with in vivo-like cell structure, tissue organization, and selective molecular filtration. The fenestrae regulate biomolecule passage by size and charge, simulating kidney function in a controlled setting. These devices allow real-time study of disease progression and therapeutic testing in a more physiological context than 2D cultures or animal models. This functionality is especially valuable for modeling glomerular injury and diseases such as proteinuria, often arising from glomerular damage.

The importance of 3D architecture and vascularization in kidney OoC systems provides new insights into kidney function and disease mechanisms. Lin et al.131 advanced this field by developing a 3D vascularized proximal tubule (3D VasPT) model that mimics native kidney structure and function. The model features adjacent conduits lined

### 2.2.2. Neurogenic organ-on-a-chip

The relationship between neurons and their target organs or cells is fundamental to biological function. Neurons control tissues including muscle, heart, blood vessels,


<!-- Page 20 -->


Volume x Issue x (2026) 20  doi: 10.36922/OR026020001

and bone through synaptic connections and signaling pathways. This regulation maintains homeostasis, enables rapid responses to environmental changes, and coordinates complex physiological processes. Disruptions in neural interactions can cause severe pathologies such as neuromuscular disorders, cardiovascular disease, and impaired bone remodeling. Understanding neuron–organ interactions is therefore essential for both basic science and therapeutic development. OoC technology—particularly models integrating neural components with specific organ systems such as neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), neuro-cardiac coupling, neurovascular units (NVUs), and neuro-bone—offers a powerful in vitro platform to replicate these interactions. By mimicking direct cell-tocell communication and microenvironmental cues, these systems provide new insights into the dynamic interplay between neurons and their target tissues.

(a)	 Neuromuscular junction-on-a-chip

Neuromuscular junctions are essential for motor function, acting as the interface between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibers. NMJ degeneration is linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy. Recent advances in bioengineering and OoC techniques offer new ways to study these processes. Compartmentalized designs mimic the body’s physical separation between spinal cord and limb, allowing observation of motor neuron axonal outgrowth and remote muscle innervation. This approach more accurately replicates in vivo neuromuscular interactions and provides a platform for studying NMJ pathology and repair in both basic and translational research.136

The study of human neuromuscular function and disease has traditionally relied on animal models due to challenges in direct human research. Ionescu et al.137 developed a simplified in vitro model to explore molecular communication between motor neurons and muscle cells using a compartment-containing microfluidic system. This platform enabled the formation of functional in vitro NMJs and imaging techniques to measure axon outgrowth and NMJ activity, clarifying the complex cellular mechanisms involved in the structure and function of NMJs. However, this study relied on mouse models, which may not fully represent human physiology.

To better study NMJ formation, maturation, and degeneration, human-specific tissue-engineered NMJ models have been developed. Uzel et al.132 created a microfluidic platform integrating myoblast-derived muscle strips and motor neurons differentiated from mouse ESCs within a 3D hydrogel. Incorporation of optogenetic control enhanced the versatility of NMJ studies: photosensitizing ESCs with channelrhodopsin made motor neurons optically excitable, allowing spatiotemporal control of

neuronal activation. This approach enabled selective excitation of motor neurons or muscle cells, providing more refined NMJ analysis than traditional chemical stimulation methods. The system’s design allows the use of light to explore complex processes such as NMJ maturation, synaptic adaptation, and muscle remodeling, providing insights into the role of activity in plastic synaptic changes. The system also used compliant micropillars to anchor muscle strips, offering a noninvasive way to measure muscle contraction and force generation. This feature is particularly valuable in drug screening, where muscle activity serves as a marker of treatment efficacy. The ability to quantitatively assess neuromuscular function, along with opportunities for further engineering, makes this system promising for advancing NMJ pathology research, highcontent screening assays for neuromuscular diseases, and applications in soft robotics (Figure 5a).

Interspecific differences limit the translation of animal model research into clinical practice. To address this, Vila et al.138 further developed a bioengineered, allogeneic, patientspecific human NMJ model. Unlike previous studies, this study focused on creating standardized, objective, and quantitative methods to detect and diagnose disease. The platform combines tissue engineering, optogenetics, microfabrication, optoelectronics, and video processing, making it well-suited for diagnosing and evaluating novel therapies for myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated autoimmune disease. Yamamoto et al.139 proposed a human neuromuscular tissue microfluidic model developed in a human 24-well plate format. This study marks progress in mimicking human tissues on microfluidic devices.

(b)	 Neurovascular unit organ-on-a-chip

The NVU—comprising brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs), pericytes, astrocytes, neurons, and the ECM—is essential for maintaining BBB integrity and cerebral homeostasis. NVU-on-a-chip models provide powerful tools for studying brain diseases, pathogen penetration, and the neurorestorative potential of therapies. Lyu et al.133 developed a microfluidic stroke model with an integrated NVU to evaluate stem cell therapies for ischemic stroke. The system incorporated BMECs, pericytes, astrocytes, neurons, and microglia, enabling investigation of post-stroke recovery and the role of stem cell types in neurorestoration. Results showed that human neural progenitor cells and human neural stem cells promote recovery mainly by enhancing NVU structural and functional integrity rather than direct neuronal replacement. This highlights the importance of restoring NVU functionality in post-stroke recovery, focusing on gliogenesis, vessel development, and immune regulation. The model also allows assessment of stem cell behavior across the BBB, making it a valuable tool for preclinical stem cell–based therapy trials. Collectively, these OoC

models support more personalized, high-throughput testing of NVU-targeted interventions and provide a powerful platform for neurodegenerative disease research and drug screening (Figure 5b).

These models recapitulate the brain’s vascular environment, including functional BBB formation, NVU cellular interactions, and responses to external stimuli such as pathogens or therapeutic agents. Kim et al.134 developed a human NVU-on-a-chip that mimics BBB structure and function by integrating human neural stem cells, BMECs, and brain pericytes. Using optimized hydrogel composition and fluidic systems, the platform recreated brain-like conditions to study microbial penetration, focusing on the neurotropic behavior of Cryptococcus neoformans. The system showed that the pathogen crosses the BBB without disrupting tight junctions, potentially via transcytosis. This model enables real-time study of pathogen dynamics and microbial–BBB interactions, expanding opportunities for infectious disease research and therapeutic drug testing (Figure 5c).

(c)	 Nerve-bones organ-on-a-chip

The neurovascularized bone chip (NVB chip) was developed to model interactions between the nervous system, vasculature, and bone tissue under inflammatory conditions. It incorporates three compartments—neuronal, vascular, and bone—that mimic crosstalk among sensory neurons, endothelial cells, and osteoclasts. The NVB chip is a compartmentalized microfluidic device with three interconnected channels for neuronal, vascular, and bone cells. The neuronal compartment, containing dorsal root ganglion explants, is separated from the vascular and bone compartments by microgrooves that permit axonal projections but block somal components. The vascular unit, formed with a collagen/fibrin hydrogel, supports endothelial cells in a 3D configuration mimicking capillary structures. The bone unit, seeded with osteoclasts, lies adjacent to the vascular compartment. This design places neuronal terminals in proximity to endothelial and bone cells, enabling study of nerve–vascular–bone interactions under physiological and inflammatory conditions. The NVB chip provides a versatile platform for investigating inflammatory bone diseases such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, mimicking the complex interplay among nerves, vessels, and bone in a controlled in vitro environment.

This model seeks to unravel mechanistic interactions in inflammatory bone diseases such as osteoarthritis. Beyond modeling osteoclasts, the NVB chip examines inflammation’s effects on neuronal function, particularly pain perception. Under inflammatory conditions, sensory neurons in the neuronal compartment show increased axonal sprouting toward the vascular and bone units,

suggesting heightened pain responses. This effect is linked to upregulated neurotrophic factors such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), secreted by endothelial cells under inflammatory signals. Interactions between osteoclasts and endothelial cells may further promote nerve sprouting through additional pro-inflammatory factors. This model provides insight into neurovascular modulation of bone pain and serves as a platform to test anti-inflammatory therapies. Using a microfluidic approach, the NVB chip provides a powerful tool to study bone inflammation, pain perception, and nerve–bone interactions in disease progression (Figure 5d).135

### 2.2.3. Multi-organ-on-a-chip

Multi-OoC platforms represent a major innovation in OoC technology, enabling the modeling of inter-organ interactions and systemic physiology in vitro. Chen et al.140 revealed the interaction between tissues under normal and inflammatory conditions by integrating the liver and intestinal multi-organ platform and demonstrating the potential of this system to mimic complex in vivo processes (Figure 6a). They also provided physiologically and inflammation-relevant evidence of gut–liver crosstalk through long-term (>2 weeks) maintenance of hepatic (e.g., albumin, bile acid metabolism) and intestinal (e.g., barrier integrity) functions in baseline interaction or cytokine responses. This integrated multi-tissue platform can synergistically enhance and generate insights useful for understanding inflammatory organ crosstalk and complex pathophysiological processes.

Leveraging advanced microfluidics, autologous organ models, and real-time biomonitoring, these systems allow the evaluation of complex pharmacological and pathological processes beyond the scope of singleorgan models. Schimek et al.141 proposed a chip-based system mimicking the transport function of the human cardiovascular system for integrating biovascularization into a multi-organ microarray (Figure 6b). The systemon-a-chip interconnects two standard tissue culture compartments and further vessel branching and vessel diameter reduction down to a microvessel scale realized by a two-photon laser ablation technique. The layout ensures physiological fluid-to-tissue ratios and generates pulsatile shear stress in a widely adjustable physiological range within a microchannel circuit entirely covered with endothelial cells using a peristaltic on-chip micropump. This system provides indicative long-term experiments that revealed stable performance to mimic the human circulatory system over two and four weeks and has the potential application for future establishment of humanon-a-chip systems. Continued progress in vascular integration, immune modeling, and long-term culture will expand their applicability and clinical relevance, marking a

Ronaldson- Bouchard et al.17 developed a tissue-chip system that interlinks mature human heart, liver, bone, and skin tissues through recirculating vascular flow, enabling multi-organ interactions and the recapitulation of interdependent organ functions, maintaining phenotypic stability over four weeks and enhancing the prediction of drug responses (Figure 6d).
