Similarly, Sakai et al.148 developed a small intestine–liver platform using hiPSC-derived intestinal epithelial cells and primary hepatocytes to explore co-culture effects, showing enhanced function for both cell types under perfusion. GoC technology has transformed investigations of intestinal physiology, drug metabolism, microbiota-host interactions, and disease modeling. Continued efforts to refine device designs, integrate multiple organ systems, and incorporate patient-derived materials will further extend the applicability of this emerging technology.

The development of Multi-OoCs is driven by the need for comprehensive models that replicate whole-body dynamics. Nguyen et al.149 combined human kidney and liver organoids via microfluidic channels to study the biodistribution and therapeutic efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cell–derived extracellular vesicles. This system successfully recapitulated human physiological responses and allowed in-depth analysis of extracellular vesicle accumulation and recovery from kidney injury, showcasing the potential of multi- OoC models for systemic therapy evaluation. Li et al.150 developed an intestine–kidney-on-a-chip to investigate the nephrotoxicity associated with intestinal drug absorption, highlighting how drug combinations influence toxicity and absorption, demonstrating the platform’s predictive power in evaluating drug-induced side effects.

The application of multi-OoCs to drug metabolism and absorption has advanced understanding of inter-organ interactions. Kurniawan et al.151 demonstrated this with a gut–liver MPS, which revealed crosstalk mechanisms modulating drug metabolism. Co-culturing iPSC-derived intestinal cells with primary human hepatocytes enhanced CYP activity through metabolic interactions involving arachidonic acid, underscoring the role of organ crosstalk in hepatic metabolism and improving in vitro prediction of drug responses. Shah et al.152 introduced a multi-OoC

platform combining the HuMiX GoC and Dynamic42 liver-on-a-chip to simulate the gut–liver axis. This system provided insights into host–microbe interactions at the gastrointestinal interface, emphasizing multi-OoC utility for studying microbiome-driven drug effects and disease mechanisms.

These multi-OoC platforms can simulate the complex interplay of organ systems, accelerating drug discovery and improving human-specific disease modeling. Wang et al.153 developed an MPS integrating alveolus and BBB chips to model the neurological effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Direct BBB exposure to the virus caused mild disruption, while medium from the infected alveolus chip induced more severe BBB damage, including endothelial dysfunction, pericyte detachment, and neuroinflammation. Transcriptomic analysis revealed altered actin cytoskeleton expression in brain endothelial cells and increased inflammatory gene expression in glial cells. The study further showed that low viral loads in the lungs can trigger early cerebral microvascular damage, suggesting systemic inflammation, rather than direct viral invasion, drives COVID-19 neurological symptoms. This lung– brain MPS highlights the BBB’s role in relaying peripheral inflammation to the brain and provides a platform to investigate extrapulmonary complications.

Unlike single-organ systems, which replicate individual functions, multi-OoCs recreate physiologically accurate connections and crosstalk among organs, making them highly relevant for studying PK, PD, and drug-induced toxicity. Gao et al.154 used a microfluidic co-culture model to study macrophage–cardiomyocyte interactions in inflammation-mediated myocardial injury. This approach revealed metabolic pathways driving oxidative stress and inflammation, enabling precise drug screening and identification of cardioprotective compounds. Ronaldson- Bouchard et al.17 further advanced multi-OoC technology by integrating heart, liver, bone, and skin tissues within a vascularized flow system. This platform recapitulated doxorubicin’s PK and PD profiles, identified early microRNA biomarkers of cardiotoxicity, and maintained tissue-specific phenotypes for four weeks, demonstrating superior predictive accuracy for systemic drug effects compared to isolated tissues.

Multi-OoC models are increasingly used to assess systemic effects of drug absorption, metabolism, and toxicity, improving preclinical testing. Herland et al.143 presented a multi-OoC platform that predicts human PK and PD from in vitro data. The system integrates fluidically coupled OoCs representing gut, liver, kidney, and bone marrow to mimic first-pass absorption, metabolism, and excretion. Using computational models with experimental input, they accurately predicted PK parameters for orally administered nicotine and intravenously injected cisplatin.

### 2.3. Integration of (multi-)organoid-on-a-chip

### 2.3.1. Motivation for integration

Organoids represent a major advance for mimicking human organ-specific, multilineage cellular composition and functions. However, their lack of perfusable vasculature and limited environmental control reduce physiological

relevance. Conversely, OoC systems excel at regulating microenvironmental stimuli, such as fluid flow and mechanical forces, but fall short in replicating complex tissue architecture and diversity. Integrating these approaches offers the opportunity to overcome such deficiencies and develop platforms that better emulate human physiology. 155 Organoids provide biologically relevant cellular composition, while OoCs contribute geometric precision, perfusion, and mechanical stimuli to mimic organ-level interactions. Integration could vascularize organoids, improving nutrient delivery and reducing necrotic core formation, a critical limitation of traditional models.16 Beyond structural gains, providing flow and electrical or mechanical stimuli in OoC-integrated systems helps create more physiological microenvironments.156

### 2.3.2. Representative organ-specific organoid-on-achip

(a)	 Intestinal organoid-on-a-chip

Kasendra et al.161 established a primary human small intestine-on-a-chip using biopsy-derived organoids, combining donor-derived epithelium with controlled luminal flow. Workman et al.162 developed iPSC-derived intestinal organoid-on-a-chip with multiple epithelial subtypes and cytokine responsiveness, although tubular geometry and mesenchymal, neural, and immune compartments remain difficult to reproduce. Nikolaev et al.163 created perfusable scaffold-guided mini-intestines with continuous removal of dead cells and regenerative capacity. The iFlow platform further introduced self-assembled vasculature for studying immune-cell recruitment during colon inflammation, while luminal accessibility remained a limitation.164

Mechanically engineered devices have further enhanced modeling accuracy. Kim et al.87,107 developed a GoC that can be coupled with a porous microfluidic setup and imitated peristalsis-like motion, enabling long-term bacterial co-culture and functional studies of inflammation and bacterial overgrowth. Sontheimer-Phelps et al.165 developed a colon-on-a-chip, reproducing the bilayered mucus structure needed for barrier function and mucus hydration signaling during inflammation. The integration of microbiota into OrgoC platforms has also been pivotal. Trujillo-de Santiago et al.166 and Ballerini et al.86 highlighted microbiota-on-a-chip systems’ role in studying host– bacterial interplay, using advanced fabrication methods and stem cell technologies to recreate these dynamic interactions.

(b)	 Heart organoid-on-a-chip

The development of heart organoid-on-a-chip (Heart- OrgoC) is emerging as a promising approach for modeling cardiac function and pathology. Combining stem cell–derived cardiac organoids with OoC technology improves structural and functional fidelity while enabling precise control of microenvironmental factors. Heart- OrgoC systems integrate electrical and mechanical stimuli to simulate native cardiac dynamics, as shown by micropatterned cardiac organoids that promote vascular network formation and contractile function through geometric confinement.167,168 Shirure et al.169 highlighted that vascularized cardiac organoids generated on microfluidic platforms can reproduce human heart functions and dynamic tissue perfusion in vitro, extending their use in disease modeling and drug testing. Min et al.170 refined this approach by incorporating cardiac fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and cardiomyocytes derived from hiPSCs within a perfusable ECM, achieving maturation and effective drug screening.

Bioprinting methodologies have been instrumental in replicating the geometric and functional complexity of the heart. Kupfer et al.171 fabricated electromechanically functional chambered organoids through bioprinted hiPSC constructs, advancing the field toward functional macroscale cardiac tissues suitable for disease modeling and therapeutic applications. However, challenges remain in achieving complete spatial differentiation and physiologically relevant ejection fractions in chambered structures.169 Efforts to improve the scalability and consistency of cardiac organoids are reflected in advances by Hoang et al.168, where micropatterning facilitated the reproducible engineering of multilineage cardiac organoids for developmental toxicity testing. These approaches underscore the versatility of Heart-OrgoCs as platforms that support both foundational research and clinical translation.

The utility of Heart-OrgoCs in cardiotoxicity studies is illustrated by Mathur et al.172, who developed cardiac MPS capable of predicting drug-induced toxicity with humanspecific responses, bypassing the interspecies extrapolation limit of animal models. Concurrently, Zhang et al.158 applied a hybrid approach integrating OoC technology with cardiac organoids to study nanoplastic-induced cardiotoxicity, uncovering stage-specific mechanisms such as oxidative stress and fibrosis, and revealing heightened toxicity under pathological conditions (Figure 7b and 7c). Likewise, Mills et al.167 combined human cardiac organoids with highthroughput techniques to identify potential therapeutics, including BET inhibitors effective against SARS-CoV-2- induced cardiac dysfunction.

Overall, heart-OrgoCs have made significant progress in replicating cardiac functionality, structural organization, and responses to pathological stimuli. Remaining challenges—such as achieving fully vascularized, multi-chambered constructs with native physiological parameters—present opportunities for further integration of bioprinting, microfluidics, and tissue engineering. These systems are poised to advance cardiac disease modeling, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine.

(c)	 Brain organoid-on-a-chip

Brain OoCs (BOoCs) combine organoid technology with microfluidics, creating a biomimetic environment that overcomes limitations of conventional brain organoid models, such as variability, immaturity, and lack of vasculature. These systems enable precise microenvironmental control for advanced studies in neurodevelopment and related disorders. Wang et al.159 engineered a perfusable BOoC platform to generate hiPSCderived 3D brain organoids by incorporating 3D Matrigel within an OoC system in a controlled manner. The top layer of the chip consisted of two parallel culture chambers

Under perfusion, the brain organoids displayed neural differentiation, regionalization, and cortical organization that captured key features of early human brain development (Figure 7d). Compared with static culture, fluid flow increased the expression of corticallayer markers T-box brain transcription factor 1 (TBR1) and COUP-TF-interacting protein 2 (CTIP2), linking the engineering intervention directly to enhanced developmental patterning. Perfusion also supported extended culture and reduced the transport limitations associated with conventional static organoids. However, the platform did not recreate a functional vascular or immune compartment, and excessive shear or unstable flow could introduce new variability. Appropriate quality-control readouts therefore include organoid size, viability, cortical marker expression, regional organization, and flow stability rather than maturation claims based on morphology alone.

Similarly, researchers from the same team used micropillar array chips to generate uniform hiPSCderived brain embryoid bodies, facilitating studies of neurodevelopment and breast cancer-derived exosome effects on the carcinogenesis of brain organoids.173

A study reported the development of a BOoC platform that generates multiple signaling gradients to induce forebrain organoids with distinct dorsal–ventral structures, closely mirroring human brain development.174 Unlike traditional methods, which struggle to form gradients and organized regions, this BOoC uses a multi-layer microfluidic chip to precisely control molecular gradients without shear forces, fostering more structured growth. Temperatureresponsive hydrogels provide stable 3D support, enhancing in vivo-like development and long-term culture viability. This approach advances neurodevelopmental and disease modeling by creating more realistic, controlled environments for brain organoid research.

A key application of BOoC systems is modeling prenatal environmental exposures, such as nicotine or drugs, which are difficult to study in vivo. Wang et al.175 showed that nicotine exposure induced premature differentiation and disrupted cortical structure in BOoC, showcasing the platform’s power in revealing developmental anomalies caused by teratogenic substances. Similarly, Cui et al.176 utilized a cortical organoid-on-a-chip to demonstrate how valproic acid exposure inhibits neuronal differentiation and impairs regional organization. The transcriptomic similarities of these valproic acid–exposed organoids to autism patient brains underline the platform’s promise in studying neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.

Beyond environmental exposure models, organoid-on-achip platforms are instrumental in addressing mechanical and biophysical phenomena in brain development. Karzbrun et al.177 leveraged a confined microfabrication setup to mimic surface folding and wrinkling, elucidating the opposing forces of cytoskeletal contraction and nuclear expansion during tissue morphogenesis. This model recapitulates the biophysical basis of gyrification and smooth-brain pathologies, providing insights into related neurodevelopmental disorders.

Integration of immune dynamics with the BOoC system has strong potential for studying brain aging and neuroimmune interactions. Ao et al.178 developed a microphysiological platform combining dynamic flow with cortical organoids exposed to monocytes, showing that aged monocytes promoted aging marker expression in organoids and demonstrating the platform’s utility for modeling immune-mediated brain aging and related diseases. However, advancing functional maturation of brain organoids remains a challenge. Incorporating endothelial cells into microfluidic designs is essential for vasculature formation. For example, cerebral organoids fused with vascular organoids recapitulate neovascular interactions, addressing necrotic core formation when growth surpasses the millimeter scale.

(d)	 Liver organoid-on-a-chip

Liver organoid-on-a-chip provides controlled perfusion during stem-cell differentiation and long-term 3D culture, helping overcome diffusion and functional limitations of static systems. Ma et al.179 designed a perfused liver-ona-chip for efficient in situ culture of 3D hepatic spheroids, demonstrating how device geometry can support stable spheroid perfusion. Wang et al.160 formed embryoid bodies, induced hepatic differentiation, and generated hepatocyteand cholangiocyte-containing organoids within the micropillar chip shown in Figure 7e. Perfused cultures showed improved viability, expression of SOX17, FOXA2, ALB, and CYP3A4, and albumin and urea production relative to static culture. Dose- and time-dependent acetaminophen toxicity linked engineering control to drug-testing performance. Remaining bottlenecks include functional vasculature, physiologically faithful zonation, and long-term stability; useful quality-control outputs include oxygen, albumin, urea, CYP activity, and tissue viability.

Liver organoid-on-a-chip technologies represent an interdisciplinary innovation that combines microengineering and stem cell biology. These systems show strong potential as platforms for drug toxicity screening, disease modeling, and personalized medicine. Wang et al.180 modeled NAFLD using hiPSC-derived liver organoid-on-a-chip with induced pathological features,

### 2.3.3 Multi-organoid-on-a-chip

Multi-organoid-on-a-chip systems place two or more selforganized tissues in connected but controllable microfluidic compartments to examine inter-organ signaling, metabolism, and toxicity. Unlike multi-OoC platforms built primarily from engineered tissue modules, these systems emphasize the cellular diversity and developmental organization of organoids while using flow to regulate communication between them. Representative applications include liver–islet metabolic crosstalk, autologous multitissue culture, and metabolism-dependent drug toxicity; their shared engineering challenges are physiological scaling, common medium compatibility, flow partitioning, and reproducible organoid quality.

A critical advancement in multi-organoid-on-a-chip systems has been recreating physiological vasculature and fluid flow to mimic in vivo communication. Ronaldson- Bouchard et al.17 developed a vascular flow–linked system integrating mature heart, liver, bone, and skin tissues separated by an endothelial membrane. This system modeled doxorubicin PK and cardiotoxicity, emphasizing the importance of controlled vascular communication. Wikswo et al.188 highlighted scaling and systems biology as essential components for maintaining physiological ratios and designing universal culture media for multi-organ systems, with particular focus on mHu (milliHuman) and μHu (microHuman) models. Schutgens et al.189 further demonstrated the adaptability of kidney tubuloids cultured in a microfluidic system replicating epithelial transport, highlighting their potential for personalized nephrotoxicity assays. Such improvements ensure that organoids retain specific phenotypic and functional characteristics over time.

Multi-organoid-on-a-chip systems have enabled exploration of metabolic inter-organ interactions, such as the liver–islet axis. Tao et al.184 developed a microengineered multi-organoid system from iPSC-induced liver–islet organoids that recapitulates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and glucose metabolism (Figure 8a). The system contains two compartmentalized regions that enable 3D co-culture of liver and islet organoids for up to 30 days through a connected microchannel network under circulatory perfusion conditions. The multi-organoids exhibited favorable growth of both liver and islet organoids and improved their tissue-speciﬁc functions, facilitating increased glucose utilization and sensitive glucosestimulated insulin secretion. The multi-organoid-on-achip recapitulates the human-relevant liver–islet axis under both physiological and pathological conditions. It displays decreased glucose transport capacity and mitochondrial dysfunction under high-glucose conditions for utility in type 2 diabetes modeling, as well as alleviation after metformin treatment for utility in therapeutic testing.

Aizenshtadt et al.190 presented a pump-less islet–liveron-a-chip that reproduces features of metabolic crosstalk under physiological and high-fat diet conditions, providing new insights into the mechanisms of type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

These systems offer powerful tools for translational research, disease modeling, and precision medicine. The gut–liver–brain interaction is associated with systemic diseases, such as neurodegeneration. Trapecar et al.191 established a gut–liver–brain chip focused on Parkinson’s disease, revealing that microbiome-associated short-chain fatty acids promoted pathology-associated pathways in the brain while influencing immune-specific interactions across tissues; they also used a gut–liver–lipocyte chip to explore IBD, showing paradoxical inflammatory effects of short-chain fatty acids depending on T-cell involvement, clarifying the role of metabolism, immunity, and injury.192 Koenig et al.193 developed a brain–liver chip that combines BBB models with liver organoids to study drug permeability and metabolism, enabling simultaneous monitoring of parent drug and metabolites across organ compartments. These innovations demonstrate the capability of multiorganoid-on-a-chip systems to model the intricate interplay along inter-organ axes.

Multi-organoid systems can be used to predict drug efficacy and off-target toxicity. McAleer et al.12 demonstrated the on-target effects and metabolismdependent cardiotoxicity of tamoxifen using linked human liver, bone-marrow, and cardiac organoid modules. Yin et al.194 established a liver–heart organoid-on-a-chip with hiPSC-derived tissues to evaluate the cardiotoxicity of antidepressants after hepatic metabolism, highlighting metabolism-dependent effects of clomipramine on cardiac function. Li et al.150 developed an intestine–kidney chip for assessing drug absorption and nephrotoxicity, enabling organ-specific toxicity testing within a connected platform.

These multi-organoid MPS will enhance patient-specific disease modeling and enable quicker, more accurate, cost-effective testing of drugs and clinically relevant pharmacological assessments by reducing inter-donor variability. Ramme et al.185 developed a four-organ chip integrating brain, liver, intestine, and kidney tissues derived from a single donor’s iPSCs, which shared the same genetic background. The four-organ chip was designed to host cell culture spaces for intestinal organoids, liver spheroids, renal organoids, and neurospheres in an arrangement mimicking the in vivo situation. The successful co-culture of the four autologous tissue models in one common medium deprived of tissue-specific growth factors allowed crosstalk studies over two weeks. The four organ models were placed in distinct compartments to host cell culture spaces for neurospheres, liver spheroids, intestinal organoids, and renal organoids. ## 3. Integration of microengineering and sensors in organoids and organ-on-a-chip

### 3.1. Integration of microengineering

Integration of microengineering, such as 3D bioprinting and acoustic bioassembly, with OoC models improves biomimicry and dynamic organoid behavior, bridging the gap between organoids and OoC systems.199 3D bioprinting strategies are gaining significant attention due to their ability to precisely control the spatial arrangement of cells or organoids. Bioprinting technologies are generally classified into three categories: inkjet-based bioprinting200–202, extrusion-based bioprinting203–205, and photocuring bioprinting206–208, based on fundamental printing principles with cell-containing biomaterials. In particular, volumetric bioprinting is one of the cutting-edge photocuring bioprinting techniques, and drawing inspiration from holography and multi-angle projection techniques enables the rapid construction of centimeter-scale 3D sophisticated structures within tens of seconds.209–211 4D bioprinting further improves this field by adding the temporal dimension based on stimuli-responsive printing ink, allowing constructs to dynamically evolve under controlled stimuli.212,213 3D and 4D bioprinting have revolutionized the scalability, reproducibility, and complexity of organoids and provided an essential tool for disease research and regenerative medicine.214 Acoustic bioassembly excels in creating heterocellular architectures with high cell density, overcoming conventional bioprinting’s limitations in cellular rearrangement after deposition. Overall, the convergence of advanced technologies into organoids/ OoC systems has significantly enhanced their precision, dynamic control, and physiological relevance.215

### 3.1.1. Bioprinting-assisted tissue emergence

The spatial control afforded by 3D bioprinting enables precise integration of multiple cell types and ECM components, essential for mimicking in vivo architectures.216,217 Brassard et al.195 introduced bioprinting-assisted tissue emergence (BATE), combining stem cells and organoid-forming cells with ECMs to guide large-scale tissue self-organization and create centimeter-scale tissues that feature complex structures, such as lumens, vasculature, and intestinal epithelia, with in vivo-like features, including crypts and villi. They utilized a syringe-based extrusion system, which, combined with microscopy-based bioprinting, allowed precise control over cellular density, tissue geometry, and the placement of multiple cell types. By controlling the geometry, BATE enabled tissues to self-organize into functional structures, mimicking organ development of various tissues, including epithelial, vascular, and connective tissues, successfully forming self-organized intestinal tubes, fibrous structures, and vascular networks. BATE was used to construct multi-tissue models, such as

gastrointestinal tubes that contained both intestinal and gastric zones. The results demonstrated the potential of BATE for creating highly relevant tissue models that can be used for drug discovery, diagnostics, and regenerative medicine, providing a scalable and reproducible method for engineering complex tissue structures with functional relevance to in vivo systems (Figure 9a).

(a)	 Bioprinting perfusable vasculature within organoids

Integration of periosteum-derived organoids with 3D-printed scaffolds illustrates how printed architectures can support vascularized bone regeneration.218 More generally, perfusable vascular models are needed to improve nutrient and oxygen transport in large engineered tissues. Grigoryan et al.196 used food dyes as photoabsorbers in stereolithographic printing to create intricate, perfusable vascular topologies within biocompatible hydrogels. The printed networks supported flow, red-bloodcell oxygenation, intervascular nutrient delivery, tidal ventilation in lung-like structures, and engineered liver tissues (Figure 9b).

To address the challenge of limited nutrient and oxygen supply in organoid cores, a study introduced an approach to enhance human brain organoid growth and integration by printing meshed microporous vessels.219 By using twophoton polymerization 3D printing technology, it created artificial vessels with dense micropores to improve nutrient delivery, overcoming the common issue of hypoxia and apoptosis that restrict organoid size and maturation. These 3D-printed vessels supported greater proliferation, reduced cell death, and enabled the growth of larger, more mature organoids. The vascularized organoids showed enhanced neuronal differentiation and calcium signaling, indicating improved maturation. The vessels also promoted the fusion of multi-regional organoids, including cortex, striatum, and medial ganglionic eminence, facilitating cell migration and neuronal projections. This method offers a promising platform for simulating brain development, studying neurological disease, drug screening, and advancing complex brain organoid engineering.

(b)	 Embedded bioprinting of hierarchical vascular tissue

In large-scale tissue engineering, constructing vascular networks that withstand physiological pressures is key for successful implantation.220 Building upon their previous research, Wang et al.197 addressed the limitations of current extrusion-based 3D printing, which struggles to replicate complex hierarchical vascular structures, and the mechanical inadequacy of existing bio-inks. Their work introduces a novel approach using crosslinkable microgels to enhance the mechanical stability of the bio-ink. By integrating these microgels into a soft GelMA-based bioink, they successfully created a material that provides an ideal microenvironment for encapsulated HUVECs and

induces the spontaneous formation of microvascular networks. The material’s robust functionality enabled implanting the 3D-printed multi-branched tissue into a rat model, where it was directly connected via surgical anastomosis to the rat’s carotid artery and jugular vein. This proof of concept showed that the engineered tissue could withstand the shear stress of blood flow, marking a significant step forward in fabricating large, vascularized tissues and offering a new path for treating organ failure in the future (Figure 9c).

In the treatment of acute liver failure, where a substantial number of functional cells are required, high-cell-density 3D bioprinting is promising and key to successful rapid vascularization.221 However, conventional hydrogels lack the mechanical strength to withstand the shear forces of physiological blood flow.222 Addressing this challenge, Wang et al.223 developed a novel heterogeneous microgel–hydrogel hybrid bio-ink capable of encapsulating high-cell-density hepatocytes and supporting the embedded bioprinting of hierarchical vascular structures. By optimizing the ratio of microgels to biomacromolecules, this composite forms a covalently crosslinked network that provides the necessary mechanical stability to resist blood flow shear and facilitates direct vascular anastomosis, ensuring efficient nutrient and oxygen exchange. They illustrated the overall strategy, which involves using this novel composite to construct implantable vascularized liver tissue for rapid functional compensation. The study validated the material’s efficacy in an animal model, offering a new direction for tissue regenerative therapy.

Other research teams have also made remarkable contributions in the field of 3D bioprinting. Xu et al.224 developed a double-network dynamic hydrogel to address the mechanical instability of traditional dynamic hydrogels during 3D printing. This novel bio-ink, composed of a dynamic hydrogel and a covalently crosslinked nondynamic hydrogel network, maintains structural integrity and facilitates vascular morphogenesis through its unique matrix dynamics, providing a new strategy for tissue vascularization. Duan et al.225 focused on bone tissue regeneration, using 3D bioprinting to fabricate prevascularized bone organoids for the rapid reconstruction of cranial bone defects. By combining mesenchymal stromal cells, HUVECs, and osteogenic microparticles, they successfully achieved rapid in situ vascularized bone formation, offering a highly effective solution for criticalsized bone repair. Li et al.226 leveraged human CiPSCs to create functional hepatocyte organoids, which were then bioprinted into a hepatic tissue model. This model demonstrated significant therapeutic efficacy in a mouse model of liver failure, highlighting its potential for clinical research in liver regenerative medicine. In a groundbreaking integration of bioelectronics and bioprinting, Kong et

This innovative device possesses mechanical properties that match biological tissues and can generate dual-mode currents to support both tissue regeneration and cardiac pacing, offering a promising solution for next-generation transient bioelectronics.

(c) Multi-material bioprinting for organ-on-a-chip

Multi-material bioprinting offers additional possibilities for creating heterogeneous, hierarchical tissue structures.228 Lind et al.198 introduced a novel approach for fabricating instrumented cardiac MPS using multimaterial 3D printing. The device integrates soft strain gauge sensors within micro-architectures that guide cardiac tissue self-assembly, enabling non-invasive electronic monitoring of contractile

These devices generated high-fidelity functional tissues and provided continuous readouts of contractile strength, offering a platform for long-term studies of cardiac function and drug responses. This 3D printing method simplifies fabrication of customized devices, reduces the complexity of traditional methods, and opens new possibilities for cardiac tissue engineering, toxicology testing, and personalized medicine (Figure 9d).

### 3.1.2. Acoustic bioassembly

Traditional bioprinting and bioassembly methods, such as extrusion and inkjet printing, excel at depositing cells in controlled patterns but often fail to reproduce the closely packed, spatially defined heterocellular architectures of natural tissues. Sonic assembly, which uses acoustic waves to manipulate and assemble cellular structures, has emerged as a powerful technique for fabricating 3D tissue architectures. Acoustic forces, particularly bulk acoustic waves, can precisely and non-invasively pattern cells. Wang et al.229 demonstrated that acoustic bioassembly can generate six-layer concentric tissue architectures resembling the cytoarchitecture of the human cerebral cortex. In this approach, hiPSC-derived neural progenitors and neurons were assembled using acoustics, then differentiated and cultured. The resulting tissue model reproduced key features of human cortical tissue, including synaptic connections and neuroelectrophysiological activity, providing a platform to study neurodegenerative diseases (Figure 10a).

(a)	 Acoustic differential bioassembly technique

An acoustic bioassembly approach addresses limitations of other 3D tissue engineering methods by enabling the construction of structured, functional tissues that retain integrity over time. Gu et al.230 introduced an acoustic differential bioassembly technique that manipulates Faraday waves to position different cell types within a single construct (Figure 10b). This method leverages cell size and buoyant density to differentially assemble cells beneath nodal or antinode regions, forming complementary or sandwich cytoarchitectures. For example, hiPSC-derived liver spheroids and endothelial cells were organized into hexagonal patterns mimicking hepatic lobules, with spheroids at nodal regions and endothelial cells at antinodes. This spatial arrangement enhanced liver-specific functions, including albumin secretion and urea production, demonstrating the method’s ability to recapitulate tissue functionality. The process is rapid, requiring only seconds, and avoids sequential printhead alternation typical of traditional bioprinting. Its high-throughput capability and tunability position acoustic bioassembly as a promising alternative for constructing physiologically relevant tissue models.

(b)	 Droplet-based acoustic assembly

Acoustic bioassembly excels in creating heterocellular architectures with high cell density using a droplet-based platform to construct tumor spheroids and other cellular aggregates (Figure 10c).231 The system uses acoustic waves to pattern droplets containing cells into defined 3D structures. Researchers formed diverse configurations, including spherical, linear, and cross-shaped structures by adjusting

frequency and amplitude. This method’s high throughput and flexibility enabled the generation of thousands of organoid models in a short time, with consistent size and high viability. The droplets were crosslinked into hydrogelbased scaffolds mimicking ECM, essential for cell survival and function. Results showed this approach markedly improved tumor model formation efficiency compared to traditional methods. This droplet-based acoustic assembly thus provides an effective platform for drug screening and disease modeling, with applications in oncology and tissue engineering. Together, these studies highlight the versatility and promise of sonic assembly for developing functional, complex tissue models. While challenges in scale, vascularization, and data universality remain, the synergy of acoustic and AI-driven workflows offers a strong foundation for future advances in regenerative medicine.

### 3.2. Integration of sensors in organoids and organon-a-chip systems

The integration of sensors into OoC systems revolutionizes in vitro organ modeling by enabling real-time and non-invasive monitoring of biochemical, biophysical, and biomechanical cues. This facilitates the dynamic evaluation of organoid functionality and microenvironment interactions.78 Key sensor categories in OoC platforms include mechanical sensors, electrochemical sensors, optical sensors, and flexible sensing, each tailored to specific bioanalytical needs based on target signals and sensing principles.232,233 Zhang et al.234 developed an integrated modular platform for OoC systems that incorporates physical, biochemical, and optical sensors, enabling dynamic and automated monitoring of organoid microenvironments to enhance drug screening and personalized medicine. The system operates within a custom-designed benchtop incubator, maintaining appropriate conditions for the experiment, pneumatic valving powered by nitrogen controlled via a MATLABdriven Wago controller, and integrates electrochemical sensors for real-time biomarker detection. Physical sensing, including flow rate monitoring and detection of channel blockages, is achieved with a data acquisition card and LabVIEW software. The platform is designed to be modular, with components such as microbioreactors for organoids, electrochemical sensors, and fluid reservoirs interconnected for seamless fluid flow. This innovative approach allows for in situ, automated monitoring of both biophysical and biochemical parameters over extended periods, offering significant improvements over traditional models for drug screening and OoC research.

Electrode sensing employs microelectrodes to interface with biological tissues, enabling the study of cellular responses. In human NMJ research, Duc et al.238 developed a microfluidic platform integrated with custom MEAs

### 3.2.3. Optical sensors and structural colors

Optical sensors based on fluorescence, luminescence, photonic structures, and light scattering enable spatially resolved analysis of tissue remodeling and molecular interactions. Organic field-effect transistors provide a complementary route for chemical and biomolecule sensing.255 AND-gated DNA nanosensors have visualized glutathione and apurinic/apyrimidinic endodeoxyribonuclease 1 (APE1) in cells and organoids, supporting selective fluorescence imaging of tumorassociated molecular states.256 Ordered micro- and nanoscale hydrogels can also organize cancer-on-a-chip cultures and provide optically accessible structured matrices.257 Hydrogel-based microfluidic scaffolds are widely used in 3D tissue engineering, including cartilage models, although the scaffold itself is not necessarily a sensor.258

Optical biosensors can convert molecular secretion or tissue remodeling into non-invasive readouts. Localized surface plasmon resonance sensors have been used for in situ monitoring of insulin secretion in islet-on-a-chip systems.259 Light-scattering biosensing has quantified tissue-level remodeling in an inflammatory synoviumon-a-chip.260 Thyroid-on-a-chip platforms provide a complementary endocrine example in which organoid function and endocrine-disruption responses are measured in a controlled microenvironment.261 Structural-color barcodes and related photonic materials offer additional routes for label-free visualization in biomimetic culture platforms.262

Structural colors arise from interactions between light and periodic micro- or nanoscale architectures rather than from molecular pigments. Cardiomyocyte-driven deformation of anisotropic inverse opals can shift photonic bandgaps and thereby translate contraction into an optical signal.263 Ordered colloidal and hydrogel microstructures

### 3.2.4. Flexible sensing

Flexible sensing technologies enable conformable interfaces for bioelectronics and structural monitoring.270,271 Datadriven inverse design can optimize the geometry and sensitivity of flexible pressure sensors, while programmed microlattice architectures provide a route to controllable 3D curved mesosurfaces.272,273 These design strategies are relevant to shape-adaptive organoid interfaces because they connect material architecture with mechanical conformity, sensitivity, and device integration.

When 2D planar MEAs are used to monitor the electrical activity of 3D organoids, their limited spatial structure imposes significant constraints on signal acquisition. Recently, flexible electrodes based on shell MEAs have addressed this limitation. Huang et al.274 designed a solvent-responsive, self-folding shell MEA that exploits the reversible solubility of SU8 in acetone and water to achieve precise encapsulation of brain organoids. The device’s three channels aligned with distinct brain regions discharged simultaneously, and it successfully detected increased neuronal excitability following glutamate stimulation. In comparative studies, mature brain organoids cultured on shell MEAs and conventional 2D MEAs revealed that only a few electrodes in 2D MEAs captured electrophysiological activity. While the spike duration recorded by both systems was similar, the shell MEA detected more spikes with a higher signal-to-noise ratio, demonstrating greater functional completeness relative to 2D MEAs.

A key advantage of the shell MEA is that it secures brain organoids without chemical or biological fixation, relying instead on the mechanical properties of its flexible electrodes. Inspired by soft microgrippers, Martinelli et al.265 introduced a flower-shaped MEA (e-Flower) that can detect spontaneous neural activity across the submillimeter brain spheroids’ surface (Figure 12a). The e-Flower can envelop spheroids; its actuation mechanism leverages the swelling properties of polyacrylic acid hydrogel by the sole addition of cell culture medium. The e-Flower does not require additional solvents and equipment to record electrophysiology for preformed 3D tissues after grafting a swelling hydrogel to a polyimide substrate hosting the electrical interconnects. The e-Flower demonstrated its potential for comprehensive neural signal recording by achieving a curvature with a value tunable by the hydrogel cross-linker concentration and choice of reswelling media. Organoid-encapsulating shell MEAs with programmable and shape-adaptive features are presented as novel technology that enables comprehensive 3D electrophysiological mapping. Choi et al.266 demonstrated on-chip-fabricated devices using shell MEAs that feature customizable geometries and electrode layouts tailored to cardiac organoids’ unique morphology for 3D spatiotemporal electrophysiology (Figure 12b). The shell MEAs displayed the long-term spatiotemporal field potential dynamics in spontaneously beating cardiac organoids by generating conduction velocity maps and high-resolution 3D isochrones. This advanced bioelectronic interface-based platform enables high-content 3D spatiotemporal functional analysis of electrophysiological findings for cardiac disease modeling and pharmacological screening.

Flexible sensing has revolutionized bioelectronics, particularly in interfacing with 3D biological constructs such as organoids. Stretchable electronics enable chronic organoid interfacing, supporting long-term and stable monitoring. Lee and Liu267 emphasized the development of stretchable electronics for electrophysiological recording from brain organoids, advancing organoid intelligence for computational models and illustrating how structural flexibility drives functional innovation (Figure 12c). These studies highlight organoid/electronics hybrids, or “cyborg organoids,” which maintain conformal contact despite morphological changes during development. This capability enables single-cell resolution recordings across 3D volumes, a significant improvement over rigid planar electrode arrays. To enhance mechanical compatibility, they advocate for intrinsically soft materials, such as elastomers combined with conductive nanomaterials such as graphene or carbon nanotubes. These materials minimize mechanical mismatch with soft tissues, ensuring chronic stability. Integration with multimodal profiling

## 4. Synergistic engineering: integrated design, monitoring, and applications

Synergy in MPS is achieved when biological complexity, engineering control, and measurement capability are co-designed around a defined physiological question. Simply placing an organoid in a microfluidic device is not sufficient; the integrated system should demonstrate a measurable gain in maturation, function, reproducibility, predictive performance, or experimental control relative to either component alone. Table 1 compares how these complementary features produce distinct gains and limitations across major MPS classes.

### 4.1. Co-design of biological complexity and engineering control

Organoids and OoC platforms are complementary rather than interchangeable. Organoids provide self-organized multicellular architecture, whereas OoC devices provide spatial control, perfusion, mechanical or electrical cues, and experimental access. Their integration should therefore align organ-specific cell hierarchies with microscale geometry, transport, stimulation, biocompatible sensing, reproducibility, and scalable manufacturing (Figure 13a).275

Bioprinting and acoustic assembly offer complementary routes for controlling tissue geometry. Bioprinting enables material and cell placement but must balance resolution, throughput, and cell viability; acoustic assembly rapidly patterns dense cellular structures but requires careful control of scale, material properties, and post-assembly maturation. Tunable hydrogels can provide mechanical and biochemical cues while supporting vascular or compartmentalized structures. Compared with conventional 3D culture, organoid-on-a-chip systems add controlled transport and stimulation, whereas 3D bioprinting adds reproducible spatial organization (Figure 13b).276

### 4.2. Sensor-enabled monitoring and quality control

Sensor integration must balance miniaturization and sensitivity with biocompatibility, signal stability, and minimal disturbance of the cultured tissue. Long-term measurements require controls for drift, biofouling,

Azizgolshani et al.277 developed a 96-device OoC platform with programmable flow, optical access, and integrated electrical and oxygen sensing for liver, vascular, gastrointestinal, and kidney models (Figure 13c). This architecture illustrates how sensor outputs can support standardized release criteria and higher-throughput drug-development workflows.

### 4.3. Intelligent screening and translational applications

Inflammatory bowel disease, including ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease, involves dysregulated immune responses and disturbances in the gut microbiota. Wu et al.108 developed a high-throughput intestine-on-a-chip with controlled oxygen conditions, intestinal cell–probiotic co-culture, barrier measurements, inflammatory readouts, and an unsupervised machine-learning score analyzer. The system ranked 12 Bifidobacterium strains for their ability to relieve enteritis-associated phenotypes, illustrating how microfluidic standardization and multimodal analysis can accelerate functional probiotic screening (Figure 13d).

Integrated MPS combines tissue architecture, dynamic microenvironments, and continuous measurement to

support more reproducible functional characterization (Figure 13e).278 When validated sensor outputs are linked to actuators, closed-loop control can adjust flow, oxygen, or stimulation in response to tissue state. In drug screening, disease modeling, and personalized medicine, these systems may improve mechanistic resolution and human relevance; however, predictive claims require comparison with clinical or established preclinical data.

## 5. Discussion: challenges and future prospects

### 5.1. Challenges of organoids

The reproducibility of organoid research is a critical determinant of experimental credibility, yet remains challenged by system complexity and biological variability. Donor cell heterogeneity—including inter-donor variation and intra-individual iPSC-derived discrepancies— significantly influences organoid formation dynamics and phenotypic outcomes. Genetic and epigenetic diversity within donor populations further compounds these challenges. Current organoid culture methods are laborintensive, rely on costly reagents, animal-derived ECM components, and non-standardized protocols. Culture

Synthetic hydrogel-based ECM scaffolds show promise but require further optimization for industrial-scale production and regulatory compliance. Additional factors, including media formulation inconsistencies, oxygen gradient fluctuations, and growth factor concentration disparities, also compromise repeatability.

Bioreactor-integrated approaches and automated cultivation technologies aim to improve throughput and reduce manual intervention; however, these remain in early stages and require significant refinement to achieve clinicalgrade manufacturing standards. To address these issues, standardized protocols, automated cultivation systems, and quantitative imaging analytics are essential for reducing user-induced variability and improving reproducibility.

Current organoid models predominantly reflect fetal or developmental tissue stages rather than mature adult physiology, lacking integrated systems such as vasculature, neural networks, and immune components. This developmental immaturity restricts their use in studying adult-onset disease pathogenesis. Firstly, vascularization deficiency remains a fundamental limitation in organoid systems, restricting nutrient diffusion, promoting necrotic core formation, and thereby limiting long-term viability and maturation. Conventional organoid systems face restricted nutrient and oxygen diffusion gradients that hinder tissue maturation and long-term sustainability. A critical obstacle in organoid development is mitigating necrotic core formation in volumetric specimens. Advanced vascularization strategies, such as endogenous vascular network self-assembly or pre-vascularized scaffold integration, have improved assembloid systems by enhancing tissue viability. Likewise, the absence of neural integration reduces physiological complexity in neuro-organoid models. Technical inefficiencies also persist in tumor-derived organoid establishment, including low success rates and difficulties in purifying malignant cells during expansion. Bioengineering innovations— including 3D bioprinting architectures, microfluidic OoC integrations, and multicellular co-culture platforms—are being developed to overcome these limitations, though challenges in scalability and technical complexity remain unresolved.

Clinical translation of organoid technologies faces complex regulatory and logistical barriers. Scaling production to meet clinical-grade specifications requires quality assurance, biosafety protocols, and reproducibility metrics.279 Utilization of animal tumor-derived matrices (e.g., Matrigel) introduces biocompatibility complications because they fail to meet Good Manufacturing Practice criteria. In parallel, advances in synthetic ECMs have

reduced batch variability traditionally associated with animal-derived hydrogel matrices.280 Establishing international consensus on regulatory frameworks for organoid-based diagnostic and therapeutic applications is imperative to realize their clinical potential. Organoid research has ethical implications spanning donor consent protocols to ontological status considerations. Conventional biobanking paradigms employing consent/anonymization dichotomies prove inadequate for organoid repositories given their genetic donor linkage, creating personalized medicine privacy risks.281 Furthermore, commercialization processes and equitable access to organoid-derived innovations necessitate robust governance architectures with explicit benefit allocation mechanisms.282,283 Implementing transparent policies addressing donor engagement, consent granularity, and commercialization boundaries remains crucial for upholding ethical standards in organoid research.284

### 5.2. Challenges of organoids/organ-on-a-chip

Organ-on-a-chip systems face major challenges in replicating the full physiological complexity of human organs. Vascularization remains a key bottleneck, as establishing robust vascular networks is essential for mimicking organ-specific perfusion, oxygen gradients, and drug distribution. While multi-OoC platforms have demonstrated feasibility for PK–PD modeling, optimizing nutrient transport and metabolite clearance is critical to enhance inter-organ physiological relevance. The lack of standardized culture media formulations or harmonized hiPSC protocols often leads to cellular dedifferentiation and functional decline during long-term culture. In addition, polymeric substrates such as PDMS adsorb small molecules, undermining reproducibility in drug screening models. Operational barriers—including high production costs and limited throughput—further constrain adoption in resource-limited environments.

Scaling organoid and OoC production for highthroughput applications also presents technical challenges. Current OoC designs face limitations due to microfluidic complexity and non-physiological media-to-cell ratios. Open-well configurations and 3D bioprinting strategies offer scalable integration without sacrificing biological fidelity. Automation of cell culture protocols further supports standardization while increasing drug screening throughput. Integrated OoC systems hold strong potential for individualized therapeutic strategies. Recent progress highlights human-on-a-chip platforms capable of concurrent multi-organ functional modeling. These systems aim to replicate holistic physiological responses, improve translational accuracy, and reduce reliance on animal models. However, scaling introduces technical challenges, including cell sourcing standardization,

medium optimization, and interconnectivity adaptation.

Operational quality control should combine morphology, composition, function, and stability rather than relying on a single endpoint. Minimum metrics should include size distribution and structural features, cell-type composition and spatial organization, organ-specific functional outputs, barrier or electrical performance where relevant, and the duration of stable culture. Major sources of variability include donor and cell batches, ECM lots, flow and shear conditions, PDMS adsorption, bubbles, and sensor drift. Alignment across laboratories therefore requires reference materials, standard curves, predefined acceptance ranges, minimum reporting standards, and cross-platform benchmarking. These measures convert reproducibility from a general aspiration into a documented release criterion for research and manufacturing workflows.279,280

### 5.3. Future prospects

Regulatory policy should be described as a pathway for qualified new approach methodologies, not as a universal replacement of animal studies. Section 3209 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (often called the FDA Modernization Act 2.0) broadened the statutory concept of a nonclinical test so that scientifically valid in vitro, in silico, and other non-animal methods may be used; it did not prohibit animal studies or designate organoids and OoC systems as preferred preclinical models.285,286 The 118th-Congress FDA Modernization Act 3.0 (S. 5046) passed the Senate on December 12, 2024, but the House did not pass it before that Congress ended, so the 2024 bill did not become law.287 On April 10, 2025, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) released a roadmap for reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies. The program begins with monoclonal antibodies and proposes phased expansion to other product classes, using fit-for-purpose validation, defined contexts of use, and weight-of-evidence assessment.288 Organoids and OoC systems may therefore contribute regulatory evidence when they are sufficiently reliable, standardized, and relevant to the specific safety or efficacy question; they should not be presented as automatically replacing all animal studies.

The synergistic engineering of organoids and OoC, along with their integration with microengineering and sensing, makes it possible to more accurately simulate human physiological and pathological states, providing stronger support for drug development and disease research. The future of this field lies in the seamless integration and synergy of many technologies. The combination of organoids and OoC with AI and big data technologies has brought new opportunities to biomedical research and precision medicine. The integration of organoid-ona-chip with AI enables image analysis and processing of organoids. Integrating with machine learning algorithms, it achieves a more efficient and higher-quality organoid construction method by identifying the spatial structure of matrix gels, fine-tuning cell culture conditions, identifying active inducing factors, and evaluating external stimuli. AI-assisted precise fluorescence coloring of grayscale organoid images from bright-field microscopy can be performed to identify and characterize cell type–specific information, helping researchers better observe and analyze the development of organoids and their responses to drugs. Digital twin organ models combined with experimental data from organoids can perform virtual simulations of real organs for disease prediction and diagnostic assistance and develop more precise treatment plans.

The integration of organoid-on-a-chip with big data analysis provides rich materials and data support for drug development and disease research. Organoid models can obtain multi-level data on the growth, development, and drug responses under different conditions, covering information on genes, proteins, cells, and tissues. In disease research, organoids simulate disease states in multi-OoC systems; macroscopic big data analysis integrates multisource data and different factors on the occurrence and development of organ diseases to mine potential patterns and conduct in-depth exploration of disease mechanisms and the development of new treatment strategies. In drug development, analyzing a large amount of organoid drug test data can be used to predict the efficacy and safety of drugs, explore the mechanism of drug action, and screen drug targets. Personalized treatment plans can also be developed for patients by analyzing the vast amount of data generated from organoids with AI and integrating clinical data and treatment experiences from big data. These advanced systems will not only deepen our understanding of in vivo and in vitro human biology but also open up new avenues for the development of novel therapeutics and personalized healthcare solutions.

## 6. Conclusion

Organoids and OoC systems provide complementary strengths: organoids reproduce self-organized multicellular architecture, whereas chips enable controlled perfusion,


<!-- Page 44 -->


Volume x Issue x (2026) 44  doi: 10.36922/OR026020001

mechanical stimulation, inter-tissue communication, and continuous measurement. Their integration with bioprinting, acoustic assembly, and embedded sensors can improve maturation, reproducibility, and functional assessment, but added complexity does not by itself establish physiological relevance. Translation will require standardized cell sources and matrices, fit-forpurpose quality-control metrics, stable long-term culture, transparent reporting of engineering parameters, and validation against clinical or established preclinical data. Sensor-enabled and computationally assisted platforms may support adaptive experiments and higher-throughput screening, provided that calibration, drift, biofouling, and model bias are controlled. Progress therefore depends on co-designing biological complexity, engineering control, and measurement around clearly defined questions. With rigorous benchmarking and responsible governance, these systems can strengthen disease modeling, drug development, and personalized medicine while complementing, rather than universally replacing, existing preclinical approaches.

## Abstract

## Background

Submergence stress severely constrains crop growth and productivity by creating a hypoxic

environment. Oat (Avena sativa L.) is a valuable forage species; however, the molecular basis of its

submergence tolerance remains poorly understood.

## Results

In this study, we investigated the physiological and transcriptomic responses of two oat cultivars

‘Chuannong’ (CN) and ‘Longyan’ (LY) under submergence stress. The results showed that after

submergence treatment, CN maintained better shoot uprightness, higher photosynthetic capacity and

greater water use efficiency compared to LY, indicating superior tolerance. RNA-Seq analysis generated

109.93 Gb of clean data, identified 16,258 and 18,067 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in CN under

submergence treatment for 8 h and 24 h, while 14,322 and 20,597 DEGs in LY, respectively. Functional

enrichment indicated that DEGs in CN were significantly associated with photosynthesis, glycolysis and

hormone signal transduction. In energy metabolism pathway, CN exhibited relatively higher upregulation of key genes related glycolysis (FBA, ENO, GPMI, PYK), ethanol fermentation (PDC), and TCA cycle (DLST,

MDH), ensuring efficient anaerobic ATP generation under submergence, whereas these genes exhibited

weaker upregulation in LY. Regarding photosynthesis, CN selectively downregulated photosystem II-

related gene PsbQ at early submergence to mitigate potential oxidative damage, while maintaining

significantly higher transcript levels of genes involved in chlorophyll biosynthesis (HemA, CobA), light-

harvesting (Lhcb1), photosynthetic electron transport (PetH) and Calvin cycle (FBA, TPI) at late

submergence to support a better retention of pigment pools and carbon assimilation capacity.

Additionally, several DEGs associated with cytokinin (CRE1, B-ARR) and ethylene (ETR, ERF1/2) signaling

were relatively highly activated, while ABA signaling (SnRK2, ABF) was relatively suppressed in CN.

## Conclusions

Our findings suggest that CN achieves superior submergence tolerance through relatively sustained

photosynthetic capacity, enhanced glycolytic flux, and optimized hormone signaling. This study provides a transcriptomic resource and insights into submergence tolerance mechanisms in oat, which may

facilitate the breeding of stress-resilient forage varieties.

## 1 Introduction

Submergence is a major agricultural disaster that severely reduces crop yields, and its threat is

intensifying as global warming increases the frequency, intensity and unpredictability of rainstorms and flooding events [1]. Globally, 50%–70% of crop yield reduction is attributed to abiotic stress, highlighting

Page 3/32


<!-- Page 4 -->


the importance of understanding submergence mechanisms to mitigate crop losses and promote economic efficiency [2]. Under submergence, terrestrial plants that are intolerant to flooding typically

exhibit leaf chlorosis and growth inhibition [3]. In contrast, tolerant deep-water rice (Oryza sativa) activates internode elongation to maintain shoot emergence above the water surface, thereby facilitating oxygen capture [4]. Plant responses to flooding include a suite of morphological, metabolic and growth

adaptations [5]. When exposed to flooding, the roots and shoots of oats are both damaged [6].

Oat (Avena sativa L.) is a vital forage and silage resource in China, valued for high nutrition, excellent

palatability and digestibility. Studies indicate that incorporating oat into livestock feed enhances digestibility and promotes overall animal health [7, 8]. Oat production in China is primarily found in the

mountainous areas of North, Northwest China, and Southwest China. Among these, the Southwest region holds particular significance for oat cultivation, with recent studies confirming oat as an

important crop in this region due to its nutritional value and adaptability to the challenging climate [9]. The Southwest region, characterized by its complex topography and diverse climate, is frequently influenced by warm, humid southwestern air currents that bring abundant precipitation [10]. However,

this abundance of precipitation can sometimes lead to submergence problems. While the responses to submergence have been extensively researched in cereal crops such as rice [11], barley [12], wheat [13]

and maize [14], the response of oat to anaerobic stress has been less explored, although emerging evidence suggests oat may exhibit superior recovery compared with other cereals under anaerobic

conditions. Studies have already revealed that initial growth reduction does not affect the harvest index of oat under temporal waterlogging [15]. Therefore, further investigation into the mechanism of oats in

response to submergence is essential. This will not only deepen our understanding of oat’s adaptive strategies to flooding stress but also guide the breeding of high-yield and disease-resistant oat varieties that can effectively support grain-forage rotation systems and meet the growing forage demands of the

livestock industry in the Southwest region of China.

Physiologically, submergence imposes energy deficit and metabolic disruption. It markedly reduces the

photosynthetic rate [16], gas exchange and carbohydrate levels [17, 18], impairing leaf and stem development. Chlorophyll degradation is commonly observed via the upregulation of chlorophyllase and

pheophytinase, which result in decreased chlorophyll content and impaired light harvesting [19]. Under submergence, plants rely on stored carbohydrates for metabolism. However, due to the low rate of photosynthesis, these reserves are rapidly depleted, ultimately leading to plant death. Therefore, a

variety's tolerance to submergence is largely determined by its initial carbohydrate reserves [16]. The decline in photosynthesis under submergence disrupts the supply of photoassimilates, thereby affecting

respiratory metabolism. In response to hypoxia, plants shift from aerobic respiration to anaerobic pathways through glycolysis to sustain ATP production. In glycolysis, pyruvate can be converted into

lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) or gradually converted into ethanol by pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) [20]. This metabolic shift, however, results in low

ATP yield and the accumulation of toxic end products like lactate and ethanol. Due to limited gas exchanges, anaerobic respiration takes the lead, which affects the plant growth due to its high energy consumption and low energy production. Thus, how plants use energy when oxygen is low, also relates

Page 4/32


<!-- Page 5 -->


to flooding tolerance [21]. Recent studies in rice and maize have shown that tolerant genotypes exhibit enhanced glycolytic flux coupled with efficient fermentative metabolism, enabling longer survival during

submergence [22, 23].

Phytohormones affect plant response to flooding stress [24]. Gibberellic acid (GA) acts as a key hormonal signal regulating anaerobic tolerance. In rice seedling growth under submergence conditions,

GA biosynthesis genes were upregulated to promote starch degradation, leading to increased soluble sugar content, enhanced ATP production, and improved energy status, supporting both aerobic and

anaerobic metabolism [25]. Abscisic acid (ABA) responds to submergence stress by inducing stomata formation and controlling stomatal movement on underwater leaves. During submergence stress, ABA

biosynthesis is inhibited, while ABA catabolism is enhanced, causing a decrease in ABA concentration [26]. Ethylene (ET) is the key regulator of submergence response. When rice is submerged, ethylene is accumulated to reestablish contact with air. The accumulated ET causes a massive depletion of ABA

levels, and this decline in endogenous ABA concentration subsequently induces the production of the bioactive gibberellin GA1 [4]. In terrestrial plants, the limited gas diffusion causes passive ET

accumulation, leading to ETHYLENE INSENSITIVE 2 (EIN2) and EIN3/EIN3-like 1 (EIL1)-dependent signaling and enhanced production of the nitric oxide (NO) scavenger PHYTOGLOBIN 1 (PGB1) [27].

Cytokinin accumulation is positively correlated with flood tolerance. It helps plants cope with waterlogging stress in multiple ways by delaying senescence, maintaining photosynthesis, promoting

carbohydrate accumulation, and regulating the expression of senescence-related genes like SAG12 [28]. The crosstalk among hormone pathways forms a complex regulatory network that enables plants to balance growth arrest, defense activation, and energy conservation during submergence stress.

RNA-Sequencing (RNA-Seq) has been widely applied to submergence responses in various plant species including rice [29], maize [30], orchardgrass [31] and cotton [32]. However, oat genomic studies have

mainly focused on drought stress [33], salt/alkali and combined stress [34], leaving submergence mechanisms largely undefined. To address this, we investigated physiological and transcriptomic

analyses of two oat cultivars ('Chuannong' and 'Longyan') with contrasting tolerance under varying submergence durations., aiming to provide a foundation for understanding submergence tolerance in

oats and guiding future breeding.

## 2 Results

### 2.1 Morphological and physiological changes under submergence stress between ‘Longyan’ and ‘Chuannong’

After submergence treatment for 6 d, significant variation emerged between the two oat cultivars. The seedlings of CN remained a certain uprightness, while the seedlings of LY exhibited severe stalk lodging under submergence stress. Besides that, the leaves of CN were greener and stronger than those of LY

(Fig. 1A). In CN and LY, submergence stress significantly reduced the biomass of seedlings; however, the reduction in fresh weight and dry weight of the CN was smaller than that of the LY. Notably, after

Page 5/32


<!-- Page 6 -->


submergence treatment, the leaf RMP in CN was significantly lower than that in LY, with RMP values increasing to 0.5-fold and 1-fold of the control, respectively (Fig. 1D). Meanwhile, the leaf AWC in the former was significantly higher than that in the latter (Fig. 1E).

Submergence stress for 6 d significantly impaired the photosynthetic physiology of both between two oat cultivars, with the effects being more severe in LY. Chlorophyll a (Chl a) and b (Chl b) contents

declined in both under submergence (Fig. 2A-B), but more drastically in LY, suggesting a more severe loss in LY. Net photosynthetic rate (Pn) also decreased under submergence, with LY exhibiting a

considerably larger decline than CN (Fig. 2C). Transpiration rate (Tr) (Fig. 2D) and stomatal conductance (Gs) (Fig. 2E) increased in both cultivars. Consequently, water use efficiency (WUE) dropped in both, and

the decrease was markedly greater in LY than in CN (Fig. 2F). These results collectively indicate that CN possesses superior submergence tolerance. 2.2 Data analysis of RNA-Seq

After performing strict quality control of the data by removing Reads containing connectors and low-

quality Reads (including removing reads with greater than 10% of N and reads with more than 50% of the entire read in the number of bases with a quality value of Q ≤ 10), at least 5.72 Gb clean data for each

sample and 109.93 Gb clean data in total were obtained. For each sample, the Q30 value exceeded 92.67%, and the GC content was 52.29%-53.75% (Table S2). The distribution of gene expression levels

for each sample was comparable (Figure S1A, Table S2), and the Pearson correlation between samples exceeded 0.7 (Figure S1B). Consequently, RNA-seq data was confirmed to be reliable and could be utilized in further analyses.

HISAT2 was used to quickly and accurately compare the clean reads with the reference genome to obtain the positioning information of the reads on the reference genome. Furthermore, the unique

mapping rate ranged from 77.61% to 83.70% (Figure S1C), and more than 66.19% of clean reads were mapped to the exon region (Figure S1D).

### 2.4 GO and KEGG analysis of two oat cultivars DEGs under submergence stress

An analysis of Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment was conducted to investigate the functional importance of DEGs in CN and LY during periods of submergence stress. The DEGs were sorted into three groups: biological processes (BP), molecular functions (MF), and cellular components (CC). The 20 highest terms were selected for plotting. DEGs were mainly enriched related to photosynthesis and nitrogen

metabolism, ribosome assembly and translation, as well as ethylene signaling and redox (Fig. 4, Table S4). At 8 h, DEGs were mainly enriched in photosynthesis (CN) and stress signaling (LY). In contrast, at 24 h, enrichment shifted to ribosome biogenesis (CN/LY) and hormone response (LY). These findings suggest that submergence stress could induce the upregulation or downregulation of genes associated with these pathways in both CN and LY.

Furthermore, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis was conducted to identify the most important biochemical metabolic and signal transduction pathways. The findings

showed that pathways such as Ribosome, circadian rhythm-plant, cysteine and methionine metabolism were significantly enriched in both CN and LY, indicating that submergence stress might activate genes related to these pathways (Figure S2, Table S6). However, pathways like plant hormone signal transduction, MAPK signaling pathway and Vitamin B6 metabolism were only significantly enriched in LY. Hence, these pathways and genes could be linked to different submergence tolerance in LY and CN.

### 2.5 Respiratory metabolism in shoots of ‘Longyan’ and ‘Chuannong’ under submergence stress

DEGs of metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, ethanol fermentation and TCA cycle, were analyzed to further study the response of energy metabolism towards submergence. The differential expression of other DEGs showed an increasing trend with the increase of submergence time. In the glycolysis pathway (Fig. 5, Table S6), most DEGs were upregulated in both cultivars, but with significant cultivarspecific differences. The CN cultivar maintained energy homeostasis by efficiently activating key

glycolytic genes, including fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (FBA; NewGene_28725) 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate-independent phosphoglycerate mutase (GPMI; Contig18770.path3, Contig23839.path2), and pyruvate kinase (PYK; Contig18138.path2, Contig19394.path1). Most notably, the upregulation of enolase (ENO; Contig9469.path1) in CN was far greater than in LY, likely contributing to a

higher glycolytic flux in the tolerant cultivar. In the ethanol fermentation pathway, pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC; Contig12452.path2) was strongly induced in CN, coordinating with alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to sustain energy supply via anaerobic respiration. CN also significantly upregulated the TCA cycle core gene dihydrolipoamide S-Succinyltransferase (DLST; Contig12757.path1) and malate dehydrogenase

Page 7/32


<!-- Page 8 -->


(MDH; Contig6741, Contig19120.path1), ensuring the supply of precursors for energy production and biosynthesis. Collectively, these transcriptional changes indicate a metabolic shift toward glycolytic and fermentative ATP production under hypoxia, with cultivar-specific differences in the magnitude and kinetics of the response.

### 2.6 Photosynthetic responses in shoots of ‘Longyan’ and ‘Chuannong’ under submergence stress

To elucidate how submergence stress affects photosynthesis, we analyzed the relevant DEGs in chlorophyll metabolism and photosynthesis pathways. In chlorophyll metabolism, genes involved in the early steps of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis, including glutamyl-tRNA reductase (HemA; NewGene_33032) and uroporphyrinogen-III methyltransferase (CobA; NewGene_23622, Contig238.path1), were predominantly upregulated in CN. By contrast, several genes involved in later steps, such as ferrochelatase (HemH),

magnesium-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester (oxidative) cyclase (chlE), and chlorophyll synthase (chlG), were downregulated in both cultivars. Notably, the chlorophyll degradation gene chlorophyllase (CLH) was upregulated under submergence in both cultivars (Fig. 6, Table S6). For photosynthetic light reactions, genes encoding photosystem II components (oxygen-evolving enhancer protein PsbQ and

PsbP), light-harvesting proteins (Lhca2 and Lhcb7), and ferredoxin (PetF) were predominantly downregulated in both cultivars, with CN often exhibiting more pronounced decreases at the 8‑h time point. In contrast, ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase (PetH ; Contig3688.path2) and the light-harvesting gene chlorophyll a/b‑binding protein (Lhcb1; NewGene_59459) were upregulated in CN, with Lhcb1 showing significantly higher expression in CN than in LY at 24 h. This indicates that submergence severely impairs

photosystem II and light-harvesting capacity, while partially inducing compensatory expression of certain electron transport and antenna components. In the Calvin cycle, most DEGs encoding Calvin cycle enzymes were upregulated in both cultivars. Specifically, fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (FBA), ribose 5- phosphate isomerase A (RpiA), and triosephosphate isomerase (TPI) were upregulated, with CN showing

higher fold changes at 8 h in TPI (Contig2070.path1). By contrast, phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase I (FBP) were downregulated in both cultivars. These transcriptional changes indicate that submergence impairs photosystem II and light-harvesting capacity, while partially inducing compensatory expression of certain electron transport and Calvin cycle components.

### 2.7 Plant hormone signal transduction in shoots of ‘Longyan’ and ‘Chuannong’ under submergence stress

Hormones are the central regulators of plants’ growth, development and responses to changing

environments [35]. In this study, DEGs related to cytokinin, gibberellin (GA), abscisic acid (ABA) and ethylene were further analyzed. For cytokinin signaling, CN demonstrated optimized signal perception and transduction, with DEGs related to arabidopsis histidine kinase CRE1 (Contig35708.path1) and GARP family transcription factor B-ARR (Contig12743.path1) maintaining higher expression levels in late-stage submergence (24 h), likely contributing to the delay of submergence-induced senescence. In contrast, LY
